items.title: When Fine-Grained Credit Assignment Helps and Hurts: Multimodal Agentic Reinforcement Learning through Video Editing
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise for training multimodal agents to reason and use tools. However, it remains unclear when fine-grained credit assignment improves learning and when it fails to improve task performance. Video editing provides a useful testbed for this question, combining multimodal perception, long-horizon planning, and tool use with delayed outcome feedback. We construct four movie-trailer editing task types---Content Selection, Narrative Sequencing, Rough Cut, and Fine Cut---that reflect real-world editing workflows and span different levels of task complexity and interaction horizon. Decaying process rewards provides the largest benefit on Fine Cut, with a 45.4% relative gain over outcome-only GRPO on tasks averaging more than 60 turns under outcome-only GRPO. On the three shorter-horizon task types averaging 30--40 turns under the same baseline, outcome-only GRPO remains competitive, with decaying process rewards yielding at most a 10.4% relative gain. Process rewards from an LLM judge initially improve tool use and encourage visual inspection. As training progresses, however, GRPO+PRM with a fixed process-reward weight increasingly exhibits excessive reasoning and redundant tool calls: process rewards continue to rise while task completion rates and outcome scores decline. Decaying the process-reward weight to zero mitigates this reward-hacking behavior while preserving the early gains. Despite dense token-level supervision, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) yields little improvement or substantial degradation and is highly sensitive to the choice of privileged information. Our analysis reveals differences in teacher--student disagreement and gradient magnitudes, and suggests possible dilution of informative signals over long trajectories.

items.title: When Interpreters Really Are Machines: The Use of Artificial Intelligence in Intercultural Health Care Communication
items.abstract: Machine translation (MT) and artificial intelligence (AI) are used in an ad hoc manner to negotiate intercultural communication in health care settings. As AI is currently subject to public debate, it is important to consider perceptions of and discourses around it. Through a literature review of translation and interpreting studies and health sciences, this article first explores some challenges that MT and AI pose, along with the persistence of reductive thinking around language and the role of the interpreter. It then develops a qualitative content analysis of 41 semi-structured interviews with health care and intercultural communication actors in Catalonia. Informants view MT and AI as useful for simple, low-stakes communication while preferring humans. Despite this, there is an ‘acquiescent anxiety’ around the unstoppable progress of science. In addition, there is a tendency to distinguish between ‘mere’ translation and other ‘added value’ activities, like intercultural mediation. We argue that, when interpreters are not merely thought of as machines, but really are machines, the relentless reduction of interpreting to ‘mechanical parroting’ paves the way for its automatisation. On the flipside, informants reclaim an expanded interpreter role that involves knowledge of language, culture, medicine, the sociology of health and illness, social science methodologies and ethical intercultural communication.

items.title: Who benefits from LLMs? Prompt engineering competence and equity in higher education
items.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming embedded in higher education, yet their benefits may be unevenly distributed. This study conceptualizes prompt engineering competence (PEC) as an equity-relevant interaction competence and examines whether differences in PEC are associated with perceived academic gains and perceived educational inequity. We adopt a two-stage quantitative design combining a cross-sectional survey with a within-subject prompt-quality experiment. Stage 1 reports a survey of Chinese undergraduates who have used LLMs ( N = 380), measuring PEC, perceived academic performance gains, perceived educational inequity, family digital capital, gaming experience, and a planning/independent-work tendency. Regression and mediation analyses show that PEC was strongly associated with perceived academic gains, while its association with perceived inequity was statistically significant but small. Background resources and learning-related experiences and dispositions explained substantial variance in PEC, especially gaming experience and planning/independent-work tendency, and the association between family digital capital and perceived academic gains was largely indirect through PEC. Stage 2 conducts a within-subject prompt-quality experiment across four higher-education task types and four popular models, comparing basic prompts with a student-oriented five-component refined prompt framework (Role–Goal–Input–Process–Output). Analysis of 400 matched prompt comparisons, comprising 800 model outputs, indicates that the refined prompt scaffold consistently outperforms basic prompts. Overall, the findings identify PEC as a potential competence pathway through which students may differ in their ability to convert LLM access into learning-related benefits, while structured prompt scaffolds may provide a scalable approach to reducing prompt-quality barriers in LLM-supported higher education.

items.title: Who Decides What Goes Viral? Social Media Algorithmic Virality and Accountability in Internal Crises: Algorithmic Logic Fingerprints and Protected Output Finality for Electoral and Civic Information Systems
items.abstract: Abstract Problem. On social media platforms and search engines, what becomes visible, and what goes viral, is decided by recommendation, ranking, and amplification algorithms. During elections, referendums, declared public emergencies, and other internal crises, a change in the algorithmic configuration that actually runs can alter the reach of civic information at national scale within hours. Once an item has been amplified to millions of people, the effect cannot be undone. Where present solutions fall short. Today’s accountability rests on deployment approvals, model version records, signed software, audit logs, and periodic compliance reviews. These records show what was approved or what was installed. They do not show which configuration actually produced a particular ranked feed or recommendation. They also cannot stop an unauthorized output before it reaches users. A configuration can be approved upstream while a fallback model, experiment router, cache, or edge service substitutes, reorders, or redirects the output on an unverified path. Retrospective audit can find such a change only after the amplification has already happened. Solution. This work describes an implementation-neutral architecture built on the Algorithmic Logic Fingerprint (ALF), which has three parts: ALF-I identifies an authorized algorithmic configuration. ALF-E records protected measurements of the components and configurations that actually executed. ALF-O binds that execution evidence to a specific pending output. A protected validation domain issues a cryptographically authenticated validation receipt. Authority to make the output effective is set up separately as a scoped, non-bearer finality enablement. An independent Finality Sink at the effectuation boundary (gateway, CDN or edge, network egress, or device rendering) reconstructs the actual pending operation. It then checks the receipt, the enablement, the current crisis-mode generation, revocation state, and route coverage, and consumes the authority atomically before permitting the output. When any check fails, the output is withheld rather than delivered. What is new. The architecture treats algorithmic virality as a sequence of individually verifiable amplification operations. It separates computation, validation, and authority: computation is not authority to make an output effective. It models internal crises as authenticated, generation-numbered operating modes that untrusted workloads cannot switch. Organic speech is protected structurally. A failed algorithmic amplification check does not block a user’s direct publication. Heterogeneous proprietary algorithms can be verified without requiring a common ranking model and without disclosing source code, model weights, or ranking parameters. The work sets out 22 enforcement points across model activation, distributed ranking stages, delivery routes, streaming feeds, and device displays. It also provides a structured counter-verification procedure for disputed decisions. Its technical relevance is discussed for the EU Digital Services Act (Articles 34, 35, 37, and 40), the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Articles 9 and 12 to 15), India’s Information Technology Act, 2000, with the Intermediary Guidelines Rules, 2021, as amended, and the WTO Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade (Articles 2.1, 2.2, and 2.4). These references describe possible technical relevance only and do not establish legal compliance. The architecture does not prescribe political viewpoints, judge the truthfulness of speech, or require algorithmic uniformity: algorithmic accountability does not require algorithmic uniformity. This work makes no allegation of electoral manipulation, unlawful interference, or regulatory violation by any platform, company, government, political organization, or individual. items.title: Who supervises workplace AI? Poland's implementation of the AI Act and the exit of the Labour Inspectorate
items.abstract: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 defers the AI Act's obligations for high-risk employment systems to December 2027, a year after Member States must transpose the Platform Work Directive. The order in which EU rules on algorithmic management reach the workplace has been inverted, and the first national implementing measures are being adopted in the interval. Poland's Act of 3 July 2026 is one of them. This development note examines what it does with the obligation in Article 26(7) AIA, which requires employers to inform workers’ representatives before putting a high-risk system into service and refers the manner of doing so back to national law. Drawing on the two rounds of consultation on the Polish bill, it shows that the Ministry refused trade union representation on the new supervisory Commission on the ground that the Labour Inspectorate sat on it as a permanent member, and that the inspectorate was removed four months later, at its own request, invoking ILO Convention No 81. The refusal stood; the reason for it did not. The episode illustrates a problem that the Union instruments do not address: representation that is present on paper, relied upon to answer objections and then withdrawn.

items.title: Who—or What—Should We Trust in the LLM Era?
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents can synthesise scientific arguments and construct computational models rapidly, but fluency is not scientific validity. Neither expert status, human oversight, multi-agent consensus, publication nor patent protection substitutes for independent empirical testing. Experiments themselves can conflict because of bias, measurement error or genuine biological heterogeneity. We propose an evidence-to-decision trust architecture for drug research and model-informed drug development (MIDD) that links verifiable primary observations, provenance and uncertainty to competing mechanistic hypotheses, adversarial AI review, discriminating experiments and accountable decisions. Credibility is evaluated for a specified context of use, not assigned globally to people or algorithms. The framework spans target validation, translational pharmacology, dosing, clinical development and regulatory assessment, illustrated by a proposed IQANOVA ATLAS AI–quantitative systems pharmacology (AI-QSP) workflow. We extend the framework to regulatory agencies using AI agents: scientific assessment and model credibility are distinct from the legally binding act of medicine authorisation. Inspired by Juvenal's question of who checks the guardians and the historical Rabkrin inspection debate, we propose auditable agent roles, explicit legal decision rights, independent scrutiny and routes for challenge. A synthetic SBML/SED-ML/COMBINE package with provenance ontologies illustrates reproducible reporting without claiming biological validation. A prospective benchmark is proposed to test scientific quality, regulatory decision loss, agent independence and appeal outcomes. The final question—whether, when and under whose authority an AI could make binding decisions—remains unresolved.

items.title: Why fNIRS Still Lacks a General-Purpose Foundation Model, and What One Would Require
items.abstract: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is almost absent from the foundation-model literature. On OpenNeuro, the largest open BIDS-structured neuroimaging repository, fNIRS accounts for 1.0% of participants and 1.6% of datasets, against 28.6 times more participants for EEG. We ask why, and what a first fNIRS foundation model would require. The paper is a review and a roadmap: its contribution is an inventory, a synthesis of evidence from adjacent modalities, and a set of requirements, not new model results.We argue that the barrier is not primarily data structure. The fNIRS data standards already require sensor positions to be recorded, so the laborious step of reconstructing where each sensor sat, which dominates the equivalent EEG models, is largely unnecessary here. The barrier is corpus scale, compounded by the absence of any clinical archive comparable to the Temple University Hospital EEG corpus, and by the recency of NIRS-BIDS, published in 2025 against 2019 for EEG. Because no single fNIRS corpus is large enough, aggregation across heterogeneous montages is the most plausible route to pretraining scale, which makes montage-agnostic architecture a precondition rather than an optimization.Reviewing four EEG foundation models that solve montage heterogeneity, we find that the two available ablations of both components rank spatial aggregation above the choice of positional encoding. Several models without a unifying spatial abstraction fall to near-chance under stringent cross-montage evaluation, mainly when encoders are frozen or tested on layouts they were not trained on. In hemodynamic and multimodal work, the one foundation model borrowed from another domain gave no uplift on fNIRS, while joint pretraining with EEG did. In the one available ablation, though, that benefit tracked the mutual information between modalities and, at the larger shot counts, fell below fNIRS-only pretraining at the lowest level tested. From functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) we take a direction fNIRS has not yet followed: recent work there has moved from signal reconstruction toward latent prediction, because the signal is noisy and off-the-shelf evaluation matters. That rationale may be particularly relevant to fNIRS, where some of the systemic physiological confounds, particularly the Mayer wave, overlap the band in which the hemodynamic signal is analyzed. We chart the nine fNIRS-relevant works we located. We identify three especially consequential properties of fNIRS with no electrophysiological counterpart (source–detector geometry, chromophore choice and hemodynamic timescale) and set out eight requirements for a first fNIRS foundation model, on which work is under way in our laboratory.

items.title: XAI for Financial Sustainability Assessment and Prediction in Higher Education Institutions
items.abstract: Financial sustainability is a growing concern for Higher Education Institutions (HEIs). Many institutions face structural financial pressures due to reduced public funding, volatile enrolment, and rising costs. Although institutions collect increasing amounts of financial data, sustainability assessments often rely on backward-looking accounting ratios and provide limited insight into future patterns. Rather than proposing a new machine-learning algorithm, this study integrates and empirically evaluates established, complementary analytical techniques within one framework: financial Key Performance Indicator (KPI) engineering, a Financial Sustainability Index (FSI), machine-learning prediction, relative sustainability classification, institutional clustering, anomaly detection, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). Using the public Higher Education Statistics Agency finance collection, we constructed a longitudinal dataset containing 2207 provider-year observations and examined income diversification, funding dependency, research activity, growth, and capital investment. Supervised prediction was evaluated on 1880 longitudinal records using leakage-safe expanding-window temporal validation. Across 1387 out-of-time observations, the persistence baseline achieved the strongest performance, with an R2 of 0.868, an MAE of 1.332, and an RMSE of 2.462. The Random Forest model remained strongly predictive, achieving an R2 of 0.852, an MAE of 1.587, and an RMSE of 2.612, while demonstrating stable performance across 30 random seeds. Temporal relative-sustainability classification achieved a mean accuracy of 0.842 and a macro-F1 score of 0.835. Unsupervised analysis identified three institutional profiles, while Isolation Forest flagged 111 financially atypical provider-year observations. Once current-year FSI was excluded, XAI analysis identified tuition dependency, income diversification, unrestricted reserves, and premises costs as the indicators on which predictions relied most. Because the FSI is internally constructed and the classification categories are sample-relative, the framework is presented as a proof-of-concept approach for sustainability screening and benchmarking rather than a validated predictor of financial distress.

items.title: Your Wish Is My Commit: Over-Compliant Refactoring in AI Coding Agents
items.abstract: Large language models are known to be sycophantic, over-complying with users even when doing so is unproductive. When these models act as coding agents, this can be costly: an agent that keeps editing after no edit improves the code writes churn, technical debt, and review burden into the codebase. Yet the consequences of sycophancy in software engineering remain largely understudied. To understand them, we run a controlled study of iterative refactoring, an open-ended task with no stopping criterion, where any edit an agent makes once the code is already clean reflects compliance rather than improvement. Across algorithmic (n=50) and object-oriented (n=10) suites, we repeatedly ask two widely used agents, Codex and Claude Code, to refactor further across five models. Over 3,000 turns, we define six behavioral signals of over-compliance. We hypothesized that a capable agent would stop once it recognized an optimized codebase; none did. Every model kept editing, rewriting up to 31x the original codebase before first stopping and resuming edits even after declaring the task complete. Over-compliance is a costly, multi-turn behavior that compounds with every turn, and our six signals give developers and tool builders a way to detect and curb it.

items.title: Zero-Shot Monocular Depth Estimation for Visual Perception in Lower-Limb Prostheses
items.abstract: Monocular depth estimation has advanced rapidly with the development of foundation models that demonstrate strong zero-shot generalisation across diverse visual domains. However, the applicability of these models to visual perception for lower-limb prosthetics remains largely unexplored. Reliable depth perception is particularly important for prosthesis users, who often experience significant challenges when navigating stairs, uneven terrain, and other complex environments. To address this gap, we introduce the Lower-Limb Prosthesis (LP) dataset, a benchmark designed to evaluate depth perception from an emulated knee-level prosthetic viewpoint. Using this dataset, we evaluate four state-of-the-art monocular depth estimation foundation models. Our results provide the first systematic benchmark of monocular depth estimation performance from a prosthetic viewpoint, while highlighting both the challenges and the potential of deploying foundation models in prosthetic perception systems. items.abstract: This academic article aims to 1) synthesize concepts and theories explaining sustainable school administration in the age of artificial intelligence (AI), 2) analyze the opportunities and risks of AI in each domain of school administration, and 3) propose a model and recommendations for school administrators and policymakers. items.title: “How Does This Thing Work?”: Mapping Citizen Developer User Concepts to Underlying Software Programming Technical Capabilities in Generative AI for Entrepreneurship and Innovation
items.abstract: No-code development platforms integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) to provide opportunity for non-technical users, like entrepreneurs, to innovate in software development. However, they still necessitate a level of coding proficiency to use effectively. A case study of building a travel mobile app with low and high tech prompts in an LLM-based no-code development platform explores how to support non-technical users by mapping technical capabilities to product needs described in plain English. The low tech prompts yield variable results in successful feature implementation and can mimic functionality instead of using the needed technical capabilities. The findings from this evaluation inform prompting guidelines, supporting non-technical users in executing their business and product needs. Mapping user concepts to underlying technical capabilities can be used as a framework to support usability of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for programming applications.

items.title: 6G Reasoning Agent Societies: Composition, Scaling, and Consistency-Time Laws
items.abstract: Emerging 6G control planes would compose Large Language Model (LLM) agents that exchange interpreted conclusions, so hallucinations can propagate even over error-free transport. Recent architectures audit each message locally against the sender's observation mask, but isolated audits miss collective behavior. Modeling the agent society as a cellular sheaf, we establish three laws valid on arbitrary topologies. First, the \emph{composition law}: network-wide divergence exceeds the sum of per-agent audit scores by exactly their hidden total correlation. This blind spot masks up to 23\% of joint divergence and, because the declared signal cancels in the cognitive signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), overstates it by $1.14$\,dB purely through topology; the resulting trust inflation preserves valid consensus states but slows convergence. Second, the \emph{scaling law}: reconciliation decouples across metric counters, so the worst-connected dimension sets the pace. Consistency time grows for a society size $n$ as $Ω(n^{2/d})$ on polynomial-growth topologies of degree $d$, and paths breach a $1$\,s near-real-time budget at $n^\ast=13$ agents, whereas expanders ($Θ(1)$) and radius-3 local audits ($O(1)$, $\approx300$\,ms) stay bounded. Third, the \emph{consistency-time law}: the timing error from omitted correlations is one-sided and capped by the worst-measured link. These laws, validated on simulated topologies and deployed LLM societies, give provable worst-case latency ceilings for near-real-time operation.

items.title: A Cross-Comparison of Public and Private Universities Perceived University Fairness, Resilience and Academic Engagement among University Students of Karachi
items.abstract: The main aim of this study was to find the connection between perceived university fairness, resilience and academic engagement among university students in Karachi, Pakistan. The cross-sectional correlational design was used, 500 young adults (males = 121, female = 376, other = 3) aged 18 to 26 and above were selected from public, private and federally chartered universities through convenience sampling. The participants answered the University Fairness Questionnaire, Brief Resilience scale and Academic Engagement scale having 3 sub-scales including behavioral, cognitive and anxious engagement. The results via statistical analysis demonstrated that perceived university fairness has a significant negative correlation with behavioral engagement, and cognitive engagement, whereas it positively correlates with anxious engagement. Resilience showed positive correlation with cognitive engagement, a significant negative correlation with anxious engagement and no significant relationship with behavioral engagement. A significant negative correlation was found between perceived university fairness and resilience. The outcomes suggest that higher perceptions of university unfairness are linked to lower resilience and academic engagement, also increasing anxious engagement among higher education students. The research highlights the value of encouraging fairness, boosting resilience and improving student engagement alongside psychological well-being in university settings.

items.title: A Federated Edge Artificial intelligence (Edge-AI) Framework For Livestock Health Monitoring
items.abstract: Precision livestock farming increasingly relies on intelligent monitoring systems to improve animal health, welfare, and farm productivity. However, conventional cloud-centric approaches often face challenges related to data privacy, communication overhead, network dependency, and real-time decision-making. This study proposes a Federated Learning (FL) and Edge-AI framework for distributed livestock health monitoring that integrates Smart Neck Collar sensing, edge computing, MQTT-based communication, and a hybrid Gradient Boosting–Long Short-Term Memory (GBoost-LSTM) prediction architecture. The proposed framework enables local preprocessing, model training, and inference at participating farms while supporting collaborative model learning without transferring raw livestock sensor data to a central server. A simulation-based federated evaluation was designed using livestock health data collected from 150 dairy cows across seven districts of Punjab, India. The proposed framework was compared with previously evaluated centralized machine-learning approaches to assess its predictive performance. The simulated FL-GBoost-LSTM model achieved an accuracy of 95.12%, precision of 93.48%, recall of 88.21%, and F1-score of 90.76% under the evaluation configuration described in this study. The results indicate that federated collaborative learning can provide competitive disease-prediction performance while retaining data locally at participating farms. In addition, the proposed edge-based architecture is designed to reduce dependence on continuous cloud connectivity and support localized health-status assessment. Because the present evaluation is simulation-based and does not constitute a field deployment, the reported communication, latency, privacy, and scalability benefits should be interpreted as framework-level findings rather than validated operational outcomes. Future work will focus on real-world multi-farm deployment, systematic non-IID evaluation, formal privacy-enhancement mechanisms, and comprehensive benchmarking of computational, communication, and energy requirements. items.title: A Gamified Mobile Application for Orthodontic Education: Usability Assessment and Impact on Knowledge and Attitude of Dental Students
items.abstract: PURPOSE: The use of gamification-based educational interventions in dentistry has been proposed as a novel approach to increase cognitive engagement and improve learning; however, evidence regarding the simultaneous effect of these tools on students' knowledge and attitude in the field of orthodontics is limited. This study evaluated the usability of a gamified orthodontic application and compared its knowledge and attitude outcomes with traditional reference-book study. METHODS: In an experimental study, 80 sixth-year dental students were assigned to the intervention and control groups. The intervention group used a gamified scenario-based application for 1 month. Usability was assessed with the Mobile Health App Usability Questionnaire (MAUQ). Knowledge and attitude scores were measured before and after the intervention, and data were analysed using a mixed linear model. RESULTS: The mean usability scores were assessed as satisfactory. Although both groups improved, significant time × group interactions favoured the intervention group for knowledge (p = 0.013) and attitude (p = 0.001). However, the observed effect sizes were small to moderate, suggesting a limited but potentially meaningful educational benefit. Orthodontic course grade showed a positive and significant association with both outcomes (p < 0.05), whereas gender, overall grade point average (GPA), and software usage history were not significantly associated with the outcomes (p > 0.05). CONCLUSION: Compared with traditional reference-book study, the gamified application was associated with modest improvements in knowledge and attitudes. However, the design did not allow the specific contribution of gamification to be distinguished from other digital-learning effects.

items.abstract: communication, and machine-learning hardware require high speed, low power consumption, and fault tolerance. This work proposes a high-speed, power-efficient, and fault-tolerant finite impulse response (FIR) filter architecture by integrating Vedic mathematics, reversible logic, and error-correction coding into an FPGA-based framework for machine-learning accelerators. A 16-tap FIR filter is implemented on a Xilinx Virtex-5 FPGA using the Urdhva-Tiryakbhayam Vedic multiplication technique with reversible Peres and controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates and a reversible look-ahead carry adder (LACA), enabling parallel computation with reduced information loss. A Hamming-code-based error correction code (ECC) module is incorporated to detect and correct single-bit soft errors without the hardware overhead associated with triple modular redundancy (TMR). Synthesis results demonstrate a propagation delay of 30.932 ns and power consumption of 2.645 mW, achieving a 5.57% latency improvement over an multiple constant multiplication (MCM)-based FIR baseline while providing single-bit fault correction. The proposed architecture demonstrates its suitability as a replacement for multiply-accumulate (MAC) units in convolutional neural network accelerators, particularly for power-constrained and fault-sensitive edge artificial intelligence applications.

items.title: A Knowledge-Based Recommender System for Personalized Fatigue Mitigation Strategies in Offshore Workers
items.abstract: Fatigue is a major safety concern in high-risk industries and can result from insufficient sleep, prolonged mental workload, and sustained physical exertion. While existing fatigue management approaches often focus on scheduling or generic interventions, they rarely provide personalized recommendations tailored to a worker’s current fatigue condition. To address this gap, a personalized fatigue mitigation recommendation system was designed to support fatigue risk management in offshore oil and gas extraction (OGE) operations. The system integrates research evidence and offshore expert consensus within a multi-criteria decision-making framework to generate individualized fatigue mitigation strategies based on workers’ fatigue profiles. The system considers four fatigue-related indicators: mental exhaustion, physical exertion, perceived sleepiness, and sleep loss. The recommendation system was applied to a real-world offshore fatigue dataset containing over 1,800 fatigue records collected from workers. Results demonstrated the feasibility of generating context-aware and personalized recommendations across a wide range of fatigue states.

items.title: A Long-Term Empirical Study of Aesthetic Differences in Female Characters of Chinese Animation: Quantitative Analysis Based on a Three-Tier Aesthetic Framework and Dual-Perspective Large Language Model Analysis
items.abstract: Against the backdrop of digital media iteration and the expansion of China’s animation industry, aesthetic discourse surrounding female animated characters demonstrates differentiated structural features across production eras and evaluation contexts. Existing research is constrained by fragmented indicator systems, single-modality data, and a lack of standardized frameworks to support long-term cross-era quantitative comparison. To address these gaps, this study constructs a three-tier aesthetic evaluation framework consisting of Beauty of Image, Beauty of Impression, and Beauty of Idea, and proposes a dual-perspective quantitative workflow integrating large language model-based text mining, multimodal visual feature extraction, and the entropy-weighted TOPSIS method. Based on 72 representative Chinese animated works, 851,217 raw user comments, and 261 standardized character images, this study analyzes the distribution of aesthetic dimensions in both narrative-comment and pure-visual scenarios respectively, and validates the methodological reliability from three aspects: inter-annotator agreement, human–machine consistency, and test-retest stability. Quantitative results reveal that the two contexts present divergent aesthetic weight structures: identity-related dimensions exhibit the highest discriminative salience in narrative scenarios, while visual morphological attributes dominate in pure-visual settings. Across production eras, the discriminative salience of static morphological dimensions shows a steady upward trend, whereas the differentiating power of traditional cultural aesthetic dimensions declines gradually. High-frequency aesthetic vocabulary presents identity-oriented structural features in narrative contexts and form-and-style-oriented features in pure-visual scenarios respectively, with an overall evolutionary trend shifting toward visual detail orientation over time. This study empirically validates the effectiveness of the three-tier aesthetic framework and provides a standardized cross-era quantitative analytical paradigm for animation aesthetics research.

items.title: A Multi-Domain Study on the Effectiveness of LLMs at Writing Property-Based Tests
items.abstract: A property-based test (PBT) checks a property of a program on many generated inputs, but writing one takes a property, a generator of valid inputs, and an oracle. LLM-based PBT writers produce all three, yet they have been evaluated only on Python libraries. We study how two of them, Proptest-AI and Agentic-PBT, generalize to ten programs in five domains: deep learning libraries, databases, system software, compilers, and LLM serving engines. Most of these programs take text in their own language, such as queries, configurations, and programs. Agentic-PBT covers more branches than Proptest-AI on seven of the ten programs with Opus 5 and on all ten with GLM-5.3-Flash. Domain-specific fuzzers cover more of the compilers and of PostgreSQL and less of PyTorch than Agentic-PBT. We filed 180 bug reports, 44 of which duplicate reports that others filed after the models' knowledge cutoffs; maintainers have confirmed 65 of the others, in all five domains, and fixed 23. We draw lessons for building and evaluating such writers: low observability hurts them, and mature fuzzers paired with LLM-written properties could check that each feature behaves as documented.

items.title: A Pediatric Emergency Medicine and Psychiatry Collaboration: An Intervention Time Series Analysis of the Length of Stay for Pediatric Mental Health Emergency Department Visits
items.abstract: We evaluated a pediatric emergency medicine (PEM) psychiatry collaborative intervention designed to streamline mental and behavioral health (MBH) patient management and reduce emergency department (ED) length of stay (LOS). Using electronic health record (EHR) data from 151,014 pediatric emergency department (PED) visits at a single urban PED in South Carolina between October 1, 2017, and November 30, 2023, we evaluated an intervention implemented on April 1, 2023 in which PEM physicians performed initial evaluations and promptly consulted psychiatry post-medical stabilization. Psychiatry then managed stable MBH patients through discharge or inpatient admission. An interrupted time series analysis with an ARIMA model assessed LOS among 8,791 pediatric MBH patients. The intervention system significantly reduced LOS by 81.3 min for MBH patients in the PED ( p < .001). Future research should replicate this intervention in diverse healthcare settings to assess generalizability and further refine strategies for improving care for pediatric MBH patients.

items.title: A Proof-of-Concept Comparison of Musculoskeletal Injury Risk Assessment Between Ergonomists and Inertial Measurement Units for Aircraft Assembly Tasks
items.abstract: Aircraft assembly requires repeatedly performing precision tasks at various heights and non-neutral positions. Prolonged exposure to non-neutral positions is a risk factor for work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs). Traditional ergonomic assessments can support quantifying these risks, but are time consuming. Wearable motion sensing from Inertial Measurement Units (IMU) could support ergonomists quantifying postural exposure across work shifts. This study evaluated alignment between Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) shoulder and torso scores from a focus group of ergonomists and an IMU-based analysis using data collected from a worker performing assembly tasks. The proof-of-concept results suggest the proposed method is promising for identifying general postural exposure trends. Differences in expert perceptions and IMU-based analysis were observed, which could arise from the video format of the observations, including the point of view of the worker or the visual context. Further investigation should consider how to present IMU-based data to support ergonomist decision-making needs.

items.title: A Proof-of-Concept Study to Characterize Bicep and Tricep Muscle Fatigue During an Aircraft Assembly Task at Different Height Conditions Using the Joint Analysis of the Spectrum and Amplitude Method
items.abstract: Overhead and awkward postures in assembly can shift muscular demands and accelerate localized fatigue. While electromyography (EMG) amplitude and frequency features are commonly used to assess fatigue, these features can be difficult to interpret independently. This proof-of-concept study applied the Joint Analysis of Spectrum and Amplitude (JASA) method to characterize biceps and triceps fatigue for select assembly-relevant tasks at three different heights using data from one experienced worker. For each task, slopes of root mean square (RMS) and median frequency were computed and mapped to JASA categories. Initial findings indicate fatigue patterns consistent with expectations associated with the task, height, and arm usage. Elevated height was more frequently associated with dominant triceps fatigue, with nominal and lowered heights more often associated with dominant biceps fatigue. The JASA method provides insight into disambiguating force increase/decrease from fatigue behavior and should be further evaluated to support ergonomic interventions in assembly work.

items.title: A RAG–LLM-Based Method for Automotive Human Factors Design Guidance
items.abstract: Automotive human factors knowledge is essential for early design decisions, yet relevant evidence is often dispersed across standards, design guidelines, regulatory resources, and research-based evidence. Designers must interpret these materials and translate them into actionable recommendations, which can limit timely use during conceptual design. This paper proposes a RAG–LLM-based method for automotive human factors design guidance. The method builds a task-oriented knowledge base from curated human factors materials, parses natural-language design inputs into structured intents, retrieves relevant evidence through semantic and terminology-based matching, and generates structured recommendations with source attribution. A prototype system demonstrated the workflow through a representative automotive HMI case, transforming an open-ended route-entry design task into evidence-grounded recommendations with inspectable sources. Preliminary user-oriented evaluation suggested usefulness for knowledge access, recommendation interpretation, and evidence review, indicating potential to support early-stage design reasoning.

items.title: A RESPONSIBLE A.I ADOPTION FRAMEWORK FOR SMALL AND MEDIUM-SIZED ENTERPRISES IN DEVELOPING ECONOMIES: EVIDENCE AND IMPLICATIONS FOR THE UGANDAN CONTEXT
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from a specialist computing capability into a general-purpose technology used in customer service, marketing, finance, operations, information management, software development, and decision support. For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in developing economies, these tools can create meaningful opportunities to improve productivity and service delivery. However, the conditions under which SMEs adopt AI are often very different from those of large firms and highly digitized economies. This paper develops a responsible AI adoption framework for SMEs in developing economies, with particular attention to Uganda, and grounds it in secondary data drawn from international and national reports and statistics. Global evidence shows that AI adoption has accelerated sharply, with 72% of surveyed organizations reporting AI use and 65% regularly using generative AI in at least one business function in 2024 (McKinsey & Company, 2024). In Uganda, however, internet penetration stood at 28.0% of the population and access to electricity at roughly 30% in recent measurements (DataReportal, 2025; International Energy Agency [IEA], 2023), while micro, small, and medium enterprises make up about 90% of private-sector production yet report only 35% technology adoption, with 53.4% of owners possessing neither a smartphone nor a computer (Ministry of Trade, Industry and Cooperatives [MTIC], 2024). This contrast is the empirical core of the paper: access alone does not explain or guarantee responsible AI adoption. The framework brings together the Technology-Organization- Environment (TOE) perspective, the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), responsible AI governance principles, cybersecurity requirements, and the development context reflected in recent Ugandan policy materials. Six dimensions are proposed: technological readiness, organizational readiness, human capability, data readiness, environmental conditions, and responsible AI governance.

items.title: A review of intelligent task scheduling models for fog computing in large-scale internet of things networks
items.abstract: The rapid growth of internet of things (IoT) applications has generated an urgent demand for efficient task scheduling mechanisms that feature low latency, scalability, and resource awareness. While fog computing can meet this demand by extending computing and storage resources to the vicinity of data sources, it still confronts four core challenges: resource heterogeneity, dynamic workloads, mobility, and security constraints. To address these issues, this study conducts a systematic review of intelligent task scheduling for fog-enabled IoT systems. It classifies the included eligible studies into five scheduling paradigms, and innovatively proposes a cross-domain framework that integrates three types of awareness, including priority awareness. The subsequent work of this study will sort out the core strengths and limitations of existing relevant methods. Finally, open challenges and emerging research directions, including edge artificial intelligence (AI), federated learning, blockchain-assisted scheduling, and hardware-accelerated implementations are discussed. The findings provide useful guidance for developing scalable, secure, and adaptive scheduling frameworks for next-generation fog-enabled IoT systems.

items.title: A Russian, a Brazilian, and a German Walk into a Bar, Ask the Same Question-- And Get Three Different Answers: Profiling LLM Perspective Diversity on Contested Topics
items.abstract: Large Language Models(LLMs) have shown strong performance on tasks with verifiable answers, but many real-world queries involve subjectivity, disagreement, and conflicting evidence. Most existing benchmarks for such queries remain English-centric, overlooking the vast diversity of perspectives held by users worldwide. To systematically study how LLM perspectives vary across languages, we curate PerspectivesQA, a manually verified multilingual dataset of globally contested topics covering 18 languages, and propose ROOTS, a framework that profiles linguistic, perspective, and framing diversity. We evaluate a diverse set of eight models covering both open-source and proprietary families at varying scales, establishing that LLMs hedge their answers in English but commit to positions in lower-resource languages. Larger models maintain a more consistent cross-lingual worldview, while smaller models are more easily swayed. All models also exhibit high sensitivity to minor surface-level input variations, producing notable stance even in larger models.

items.title: A Scoping Review of Wayfinding and Navigation Approaches for Supporting Mobility in People Who Are Blind or Visually Impaired
items.abstract: Independent mobility is essential to the daily lives of the growing population of people who are blind or visually impaired (PBVI). Although research on assistive mobility has expanded rapidly, limitations and challenges identified through empirical evaluations remain insufficiently synthesized. This scoping review examines 50 studies to investigate how PBVI wayfinding and navigation approaches have been empirically evaluated and to synthesize their reported shortcomings. In this review, wayfinding refers to route planning and environmental understanding, whereas navigation refers to real-time movement during travel. Four recurring themes emerged: device appearance, hardware and software performance, user interaction, and integration into daily life. We further identify critical questions that highlight gaps between existing approaches and user expectations. Based on these themes and cross-study implications, we develop a practical checklist that translates concerns from prior evaluations into actionable considerations for the future design and evaluation of assistive mobility technologies for PBVI.

items.title: A Scoping Review on Rehabilitation Systems Adopting Artificial Intelligence to Boost Motivation
items.abstract: Physical rehabilitation helps patients recover from injury and regain functional independence, but social and structural determinants of health, including living conditions, income, and transportation, can limit access to in-person care. Telerehabilitation addresses many of these barriers by enabling patients to complete therapy at home while supporting remote monitoring. However, the lack of direct supervision may reduce patient engagement, motivation, and adherence to prescribed exercises. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer opportunities to develop adaptive, personalized rehabilitation systems that enhance the effectiveness of self-directed therapy. This scoping review examines current developments in AI-driven rehabilitation, focusing on the techniques used, evaluation methods employed, and user experiences reported across studies. By synthesizing recent research, the review identifies emerging trends, common challenges, and opportunities for future AI-enabled telerehabilitation systems that improve patient engagement and support long-term rehabilitation outcomes.

items.title: A Signal Detection Analysis of Visuo-Tactile Dual-Tasking Performance Under Varying Temporal Task Loads
items.abstract: This study examined whether tactile detection reduces dual-task costs compared to visual detection when paired with a visual tracking task, and whether this advantage persists as temporal task load increases. Thirty-eight participants completed a visual tracking task and a detection task concurrently. The detection task was presented either visually or tactually, and temporal task load was manipulated by varying the stimulus presentation rate. Performance was analyzed using signal detection theory measures to determine whether differences between visual and tactile detection reflected changes in perceptual sensitivity, response bias, or both. Tactile detection produced smaller dual-task costs than visual detection across hit rate, false alarm rate, sensitivity, and response bias. Critically, tactile detection better preserved sensitivity under dual-task conditions, suggesting reduced perceptual competition with the visual tracking task. However, higher temporal load still degraded performance in the tactile condition. These findings support multimodal interface design while highlighting limits of modality diversification.

items.title: A thermodynamic correction layer for machine learning interatomic potentials
items.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials enable atomistic simulations with near \textit{ab initio} accuracy over large length and time scales. Foundation models extend this capability across the periodic table but inherit the thermodynamic description of the electronic structure methods used to generate their training data. Small errors in relative phase stability can therefore produce large errors in transformation temperatures. We introduce an additive thermodynamic correction layer that shifts phase free energies towards an assessed reference without retraining or modifying the base potential. A first order thermodynamic construction converts the required phase free energy shifts directly into configuration energy targets, which are fitted using a linear atomic cluster expansion and refined iteratively from measured free energies. We apply the method to melting and solid to solid transformations across elements with different crystal structures using a foundation GRACE model. After the correction, all transformation temperatures lie within the prescribed tolerance of the assessed values, including Ca, Ti, and Zr, where a solid to solid transition and melting are corrected together. Static energy curves, bulk moduli, and liquid structure remain close to those of the base model. Vacancy formation energies, thermal expansion, and liquid density depend on the corrected phase balance and change where the correction is large. The method requires neither retraining, differentiable dynamics, nor access to the parameters of the base potential. It provides a modular route for combining transferable atomistic models with assessed phase thermodynamics.

items.title: A Trustworthiness Assessment Method for AIGC-Based Animation Translation of Traditional Narrative Images in Architectural Decoration
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) image-to-video systems have lowered the technical threshold for presenting traditional cultural content in motion, while generated motion may alter characters, props, narrative relationships, craft features, composition, and symbols. This study implements a trustworthiness assessment workflow for traditional narrative images in architectural decoration, linking cultural evidence dossiers, sample-adapted prompts, computer-vision measurements, and blinded human coding. Eight source images were used to generate 120 videos under three prompt conditions, with five outputs per image–condition cell. Four coders assessed the videos, five experts reviewed the coding instrument, and two new coders independently assessed 48 videos. Primary deviation rates were 7.12%, 7.37%, and 9.07% for conditions A, B, and C, respectively, with no significant blocked difference after correction (Friedman χ2(2) = 1.400; Holm-adjusted p = 1.000). Mean item-level Krippendorff’s alpha was 0.250 across 14 estimable items; the independent-review composite ICC (A,1) was 0.402. Additional analyses examined coder sensitivity and the grouped generation structure. The original association involving inter-frame stability SSIM was not supported in within-image–condition comparisons (ρ = −0.052; permutation p = 0.610). An exploratory association was observed between source-image SSIM and human-coded deviations within these cells (ρ = −0.366; Holm-adjusted permutation p = 0.021). The study provides a documented procedure for comparing generated outputs and identifies limits in prompt effectiveness and the reproducibility of human judgments.

items.title: A Truthful-in-Expectation 2-Approximation for Pair-Specific Cascade Auctions in AI-Generated Content
items.abstract: Generative AI interfaces can insert sponsored content at multiple points in an answer, where click-through rates (CTRs) depend on the advertiser-position pair. Under the cascade model, users read ads sequentially and stop after their first click, so both ad assignment and display order affect welfare. For arbitrary pair-specific CTRs, Balseiro et al. (WWW 2026) gave a $4/(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation whose monotonicity has not been established, and a monotone $O(\log m)$-approximation for $m$ candidate positions. Earlier truthful constant-factor mechanisms require factorized CTR models and do not apply. Whether monotonicity is compatible with a constant-factor approximation in this general setting was left open by that work. We give a polynomial-time mechanism for arbitrary pair-specific CTRs and any limit on displayed ads that is truthful and individually rational in expectation and achieves a 2-approximation to optimal cascade welfare. Our mechanism selects an advertiser-position matching and a designated last ad, then randomly thins earlier ads so that each selected ad's expected cascade CTR is the same fraction of its standalone CTR. This yields an exact closed-form expression for expected welfare, which we maximize over a bid-independent lottery range using linear programming. Exact optimization ensures monotonicity, while a random-prefix decomposition proves the factor-two guarantee, which is tight for this range. We also show that exactly optimizing the previous welfare surrogate can violate monotonicity, and evaluate welfare and running time on synthetic instances.

items.title: A Verification Study: Comparing Human and Large Language Model Approaches to Extract Alzheimer’s Disease Determinants
items.abstract: As Alzheimer’s disease (AD) research continues to expand rapidly, synthesizing evidence on AD determinants across large scientific databases has become increasingly difficult at scale. This verification study compares human manual extraction with a Large Language Model (LLM) approach for identifying AD determinants from 10 systematic reviews retrieved from the Web of Science database. Two parallel extraction workflows were applied to the same source material. The human researcher identified 81 distinct determinants, whereas the LLM identified 74, with 44 human determinants and 41 LLM determinants overlapping across both approaches. While both methods showed strong alignment on well-established behavioral and lifestyle risk factors, the LLM frequently consolidated clinically distinct variables into broader umbrella categories, a pattern termed lossy consolidation. Although the LLM demonstrated major advantages in efficiency and quantitative evidence retrieval, the findings support hybrid evidence-synthesis workflows in which LLM extraction is combined with targeted human validation to preserve determinant-level clinical specificity.

items.title: Adaptive Pre-Ictal Prediction of Epileptic Seizures Using Lightweight SLT-SNN Framework Validated on Local Clinical Data
items.abstract: Epileptic seizures affect approximately 1% of the global population, causing significant physical, cognitive, and psychological harm. Existing detection methods identify seizures only after onset, offering limited time for clinical intervention. Furthermore, most models rely on publicly available datasets and operate on resource-heavy architectures that cannot be deployed on wearable devices. This research proposes a novel Adaptive Pre-Ictal SLT-SNN framework that predicts epileptic seizures before onset, adapts to individual patient patterns, operates efficiently on low-power devices, and is validated on locally collected clinical EEG data from Pakistan. The proposed model integrates Slantlet Transform (SLT) for enhanced feature extraction with Spiking Neural Networks (SNN) for biologically inspired, energy-efficient classification. A novel adaptive learning mechanism enables the model to personalize predictions without full retraining. Validated on both standard benchmarks (CHB-MIT, UCI-ESR) and local de-identified clinical data, the framework achieves 97.2% pre-ictal prediction accuracy and maintains 94.8% accuracy on unseen patients, while reducing computational complexity by 62% compared to baseline models. items.title: Adaptive Stream Processing Architecture Inspired by Human Cognitive Constraints and Bounded Rationality
items.abstract: This paper proposes an adaptive stream processing architecture inspired by human cognitive constraints and bounded rationality to address information overload in high-throughput environments. Conventional stream processing architectures typically enforce uniform, full-context parsing, which leads to computational saturation, token explosions, and brittle exception-handling under extreme workloads. Rather than treating cognitive limitations as operational deficiencies, the proposed framework formalizes them as evolved resource-allocation strategies. The architecture introduces five functionally distinct processing modes: 1. Keyword Scanning (semantic compression) 2. Defensive Suppression (stability preservation) 3. Gestalt Peripheral Monitoring (macroscopic situation awareness) 4. Internal Loop Prioritization (internal resource reallocation) 5. Exploratory Sampling (search space diversity preservation via hash, random, or heuristic methods) Additionally, the framework integrates macro-level clustering with minority signal preservation to ensure simultaneous data compression and anomaly retention. By converting system saturation from a terminal exception into a controlled, adaptive mode transition, this methodology provides an engineering foundation for building resilient, context-aware information systems operating under persistent overload.

items.title: Adoption of Wearables in the Construction Industry: A Survey of Stakeholders’ Perspectives
items.abstract: Despite the high safety risks in construction, on-site adoption of wearable technologies remains low, particularly in the Global South. This mixed-methods study examines construction stakeholders’ perceptions of WT adoption in Lebanon and the GCC, comparing findings with Global North benchmark studies. Data were collected via surveys and semi-structured interviews targeting 101 consulting and contracting professionals. Findings reveal high recognition of WT benefits, specifically for risk reduction ( M = 4 . 40 ) and hazard monitoring, primarily driven by safety-first motivations ( 67 . 3 % ). However, adoption remains low, with 63 . 4 % reporting minimal site usage ( < 25 % ). Primary barriers include privacy concerns ( 83 . 2 % ), implementation costs ( 77 . 2 % ), and trust or surveillance issues. Furthermore, adoption in the Middle East faces unique organizational and cultural challenges. Stronger regulatory frameworks and trust-building strategies are vital to accelerating practical WT integration.

items.title: ADReasoner: Acoustic-Linguistic Cue-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Explainable Alzheimer's Disease Detection from Speech
items.abstract: Speech-based Alzheimer's Disease (AD) detection holds significant promise due to its scalable and non-invasive nature. However, current Speech Large Language Models (SpeechLLMs), similar to conventional AD detection systems, still treat AD detection primarily as a simple categorical classification task. This paradigm provides limited interpretability of predictions, while leaving the inherent expressiveness and reasoning capabilities of SpeechLLMs largely underutilized. In this work, we take the first step toward reframing AD detection as a deep reasoning task via Reinforcement Learning (RL). We propose ADReasoner, an RL-enhanced SpeechLLM designed to generate accurate diagnostic predictions with interpretable rationales grounded in fine-grained acoustic-linguistic cues. To achieve this, we first systematically construct ADCoT-7K, an AD speech reasoning dataset combining real data and our quality-filtered synthetic data, where each instance features Chain-of-Thought (CoT) annotations and detailed captions. Second, observing the weak perception of AD-related acoustic-linguistic cues in current SpeechLLMs, we leverage Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to develop a cue-perception-enhanced foundation model, ADReasoner-Base, thereby improving AD speech understanding. Third, alongside two standard rule-based rewards, we introduce a reasoning reward and a reasoning-label consistency reward into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for RL. Furthermore, a shrinkage mechanism is employed to suppress misleading reasoning signals, while a gating mechanism progressively introduces both rewards to stabilize policy training. Experiments on three AD datasets (Pitt, PROCESS-1, PROCESS-2) demonstrate that ADReasoner outperforms previous state-of-the-art models in both detection performance and explanation quality, advancing AD detection toward interpretable reasoning from speech.

items.title: Advanced AI-Powered Intrusion Detection System for Cybersecurity and Network Protection
items.abstract: Modern computer networks face a wide range of threats, including denial-of-service attacks, port scanning, brute-force attempts, botnet activity, and previously unseen malicious behaviour. Traditional signature-based intrusion detection systems can identify known patterns but may struggle when attack behaviour changes or has no existing signature. This paper reviews how Artificial Intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning can strengthen intrusion detection and network protection. It presents a conceptual layered framework combining network-flow collection, data preparation, AI-based classification, anomaly detection, explainable alerts, and human-supervised response. The paper discusses commonly used approaches such as decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, neural networks, and anomaly-detection models, alongside evaluation measures including precision, recall, F1-score, false-positive rate, and detection latency. Public benchmark datasets such as CICIDS2017 can support controlled evaluation, but their limitations mean that results must not be assumed to transfer directly to live networks. This is a literature-based conceptual study; it does not claim to have trained or experimentally validated a new model. The paper concludes that an effective AI-powered IDS requires reliable data, careful validation, privacy protection, analyst oversight, and continuous monitoring

items.title: AGENS: Agentic Link Construction for Environment and Intent Aware 6G Communication
items.abstract: The emergence of diverse intelligent services is driving 6G networks toward an intelligent communication ecosystem with increasingly complex operating scenarios. However, existing AI-based communication methods mainly focus on isolated tasks or individual physical-layer mod- ules, which is insufficient for AI-native 6G systems that must jointly perceive dynamic environments, understand specific user intents, coordinate multiple coupled PHY-layer modules, and remain compatible with existing communication infrastructures. To address this gap, this paper, for the first time, explores auto- matic environment- and intent-aware full-link construction, which aims to generate executable PHY-layer configurations according to channel conditions and service requirements. We propose AGENS, an agentic communication decision-making framework for AI-native 6G link construction. Rather than replacing the existing PHY-layer protocol stack with a black-box end-to-end model, AGENS operates on top of the modular communication framework and jointly optimizes end-to-end PHY-layer configu- rations. Specifically, AGENS encodes CSI and natural-language user instructions, aligns communication states with user intents through cross-modal fusion, and leverages a pretrained LLM for intent-aware reasoning. An LSTM-based sequential action generator further captures dependencies among coupled sub- actions and produces structured full-link strategies. To enable stable training in the high-dimensional discrete action space, AGENS adopts a two-stage learning framework, where heuristic supervised initialization is followed by multi-objective reinforce- ment learning to jointly optimize reliability, throughput, and power consumption.

items.title: AI Based Air Quality Monitoring and Pollution Prediction: A Review of IoT Enabled Systems for Sustainable Environmental Management
items.abstract: Air pollution has emerged as a major environmental and public health concern, necessitating effective and continuous monitoring and accurate prediction of pollutant concentrations. The integration of the Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and Machine Learning (ML) offers promising solutions for real-time air quality monitoring, pollution forecasting, and proactive environmental management. This study examines the application of IoT-enabled sensor networks and AI-based predictive models in industrial and smart city environments through a secondary, desk-based review of three recent studies. The review analyses sensor-based data collection, machine learning algorithms, predictive performance, practical applications, and implementation challenges. The findings indicate that Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks demonstrate strong predictive performance for time-dependent pollution data, while Random Forest models provide competitive results for specific pollutants, particularly particulate matter (PM2.5). The reviewed industrial application highlights the potential of AI-driven forecasting to support automated ventilation and early intervention, whereas the smart city application demonstrates the usefulness of predictive analytics in urban air quality management and evidence-based policymaking. Despite these benefits, challenges related to data quality, sensor calibration, scalability, system integration, and model interpretability remain significant. The study recommends improved sensor standardisation, hybrid modelling approaches, and Explainable AI techniques to enhance the reliability and practical adoption of these systems. It concludes that integrating IoT and AI can strengthen pollution control, protect public health, and support sustainable environmental management.

items.title: AI Brown and AI Koditex: LLM-generated corpora comparable to human-written corpora of English and Czech texts
items.abstract: This article presents two corpora of English and Czech texts generated by large language models (LLMs). The motivation is to create a resource for comparing human-written texts with LLM-generated text linguistically. Emphasis was placed on ensuring these resources are multi-genre and diverse in terms of topics, authors, and text types, while maintaining comparability with existing human-created corpora. These generated corpora replicate reference human corpora: BE21 by Paul Baker, which is a modern version of the original Brown Corpus, and the Koditex corpus that also follows the Brown Corpus tradition but in Czech. The new corpora were generated using models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Alphabet, Meta, and DeepSeek, ranging from GPT-3 (davinci-002) to GPT−4.5, and are tagged according to the Universal Dependencies standard (i.e., they are tokenized, lemmatized, and morphologically and syntactically annotated). The subcorpus size varies by model used (the English part contains, on average, 864k tokens per model and 27 M tokens altogether; the Czech part contains on average 768k tokens per model, 21.5M tokens altogether). The corpora are freely available for download under the CC BY 4.0 license (the annotated data are under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license) and are also accessible through the search interface of the Czech National Corpus.

items.title: AI-Assisted Feedback and Perceived Academic Performance: The Mediating Roles of Digital Motivation and Self-Regulated Learning Among Indonesian University Students
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence in digital learning presents new opportunities to improve the quality of academic feedback, although its educational value may be associated with students’ motivational and self-regulatory characteristics. This study examined the relationships among AI-assisted feedback, digital motivation, self-regulated learning, and perceived academic performance of university students. Survey data were obtained from 337 students at two private universities in Makassar, Indonesia. The measurement model was evaluated through confirmatory factor analysis in LISREL 8.7 using the full eligible sample, whereas the structural model and mediation pathways were tested in AMOS 24 using 290 cases after multivariate outlier screening. The qualitative phase involved semi-structured interviews with 15 purposively selected students to explain and contextualise the quantitative findings. The interview data were analysed using a theory-informed thematic analysis. Results showed that perceived AI-assisted feedback was positively associated with digital motivation and self-regulated learning. Digital motivation was positively associated with self-regulated learning, while both digital motivation and self-regulated learning were positively associated with perceived academic performance. Indirect associations were significant through digital motivation, through self-regulated learning, and sequentially through digital motivation and self-regulated learning. Qualitative findings showed that students valued AI-assisted feedback for error identification, revision guidance, progress monitoring, and reflection. However, one participant reported that some suggestions were overly general and required lecturer validation. The results indicate that AI-assisted feedback might be more educationally valuable when accompanied by critical feedback evaluation, reflective revision, and support for self-regulated learning. Because the design was cross-sectional and the outcome was self-reported, the findings should be interpreted as statistical associations rather than causal effects.

items.title: AI-Driven Phishing Website Detection: An Empirical Evaluation of Machine Learning Algorithms and Feature-Based Classification
items.abstract: Phishing websites are a major cybersecurity threat because they imitate legitimate websites to deceive users into revealing sensitive information, including passwords, financial details, and personal data. Traditional phishing detection techniques, such as blocklists and manually defined rules, may fail to identify newly created or rapidly modified malicious websites. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) offer a data-driven approach to identifying suspicious websites through the analysis of URL characteristics and other website-related features. This paper presents an empirical evaluation framework for comparing machine learning algorithms for phishing website detection. The proposed study uses the publicly available UCI Phishing Websites dataset, which contains 11,055 instances and 30 predictive features. Four supervised learning algorithms—Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machine—are selected for comparative evaluation. The methodology incorporates data preprocessing, stratified training and testing, cross-validation, feature-importance analysis, and multiple performance metrics, including precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC. Existing research indicates that ensemble learning methods, particularly Random Forest, are promising for this classification task; however, performance depends on dataset characteristics and experimental design. Since no new model execution was conducted for this manuscript, numerical experimental results are not claimed. The proposed framework supports reproducible evaluation and highlights the importance of temporal validation, interpretable predictions, and real-world testing in developing reliable phishing detection systems.

items.title: AI-Generated Educational Content and Copyright Protection under NEP 2020: Legal Challenges and Regulatory Gaps in India
items.abstract: The National Education Policy 2020 commits India to a digitally delivered, openly licensed education system built on repositories such as DIKSHA and SWAYAM, whose architecture presupposes that someone - a teacher, an institution, an author - holds clear, licensable rights in the content those repositories host. That presupposition is now in tension with a faster-moving development: generative artificial intelligence tools are already drafting, translating, and illustrating educational content across Indian schools and universities, often without any settled answer to whether the resulting material is protected by copyright at all, and if so, whose. This chapter examines that tension through India's still-unsettled copyright law on artificial intelligence, read specifically through the lens of educational content rather than commercial creative industries. It traces the Copyright Act 1957's computer-generated-work provision, Section 2(d)(vi), against the Copyright Office's 2020 registration and subsequent withdrawal notice concerning the RAGHAV-assisted work Suryast; the Delhi High Court's July 2026 interim ruling in ANI Media v. OpenAI on fair dealing under Section 52; and the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade's December 2025 working paper proposing mandatory blanket licensing for AI training data, which addresses only the input side of the problem and leaves authorship of AI-generated output for a still-unpublished Part II. Comparing India's position with the United States' human-authorship doctrine, the European Union's transparency-based regime under the AI Act, and China's mandatory content-labelling rules, the chapter argues that Indian education sits at the intersection of two distinct regulatory gaps - an unresolved general question of AI authorship, and an education policy architecture that has not yet asked that question in sector-specific terms - and that closing the second gap need not wait on the first.

items.title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Liver Lesion Segmentation and Structured Radiology Reporting
items.abstract: Despite advances in automated liver lesion segmentation, a gap remains between image-derived predictions and clinically interpretable radiology reports. Bridging this gap requires quantitative measurements that are both reproducible and traceable. We present an evidence-grounded agentic AI framework that connects liver and lesion segmentation with deterministic quantification and structured reporting. TotalSegmentator-based nnU-Net models delineate the liver, Couinaud segments, and lesions, while computational tools extract volumes, dimensions, counts, and anatomical locations. A large language model (LLM) organizes these measurements into a predefined reporting schema, with numerical consistency checks against source measurements. On 51 LiTS cases, the segmentation stage achieved a liver Dice score of 0.947, lesion sensitivity of 75.6%, and positive predictive value of 68.9%. Exploratory screening of 25,494 MERLIN reports identified 10,208 (40.0%) with liver-related abnormalities. By connecting quantitative imaging evidence with agentic report generation, this work takes a step toward human-centered medical AI that prioritizes traceability and clinical relevance.

items.title: AN INTEGRATED AUTOMATED SAFETY MONITORING SYSTEM FOR SHOPPING CENTERS
items.abstract: the article proposes a conceptual architecture and processing methodology for an integrated automated safety monitoring system for shopping centers. The safety systems of such buildings (video surveillance, fire alarm, access control) are often operated as separate subsystems, so personnel must correlate events from several interfaces manually, which can delay incident recognition. The proposed approach combines a layered architecture, a unified event model, rule-based and analytics-based incident detection, cross-subsystem correlation, a conceptual incident classification, and an incident lifecycle from data acquisition to event logging. The study is conceptual and has not been validated experimentally. The expected effect is better situational awareness, lower operator workload, and unified incident records.

items.title: An Integrated Multimodal Framework for Measuring Physical Team Processes During State Emergency Operations Center Activation
items.abstract: An emergency operations center (EOC) is the central hub of activity during a coordinated disaster response. The layout of an EOC must be intuitive, conducive to communication, and free of distractions. We use a mix of objective and subjective measures to inform layout decisions that aid interagency coordination, build effective transactive memory systems, and create resilient teams. We observed an annual drill at an EOC involving 65 individuals. Subjective responses indicate that the physical arrangement of the EOC may be of little importance, given participants’ willingness to move. Audio analysis reveals high degrees of centrality, despite uneven speaking shares, suggesting all speakers within EOC subgroups contribute to group-work. Video analysis exhibits strong temporal consistency, though future work is needed to improve detection confidence. Results demonstrate the plausibility of deploying multimodal methodologies to an EOC, as we find moderate success with video-based metrics and sensitivity to intra-team dynamics with audio recordings.
