items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Green Chemistry: Sustainable Science Education under NEP 2020 - Dr Shailesh Kumar Mishra.
items.abstract: India's chemical sector, worth an estimated $300 billion and contributing roughly seven per cent of national GDP, sits at an unusual junction: it is simultaneously one of the country's most consequential engines of economic growth and one of its least regulated sources of solvent waste, energy-intensive processing, and hazardous by-product generation, with no REACH-equivalent statutory framework yet in place to govern any of it. Globally, artificial intelligence is already reshaping the discipline that promises to resolve that tension - green chemistry - through machine-learning models that predict reaction yield and selectivity before a single flask is used, generative platforms that screen thousands of candidate solvents and catalysts in silico, and autonomous laboratories that compress materials-discovery timelines historically measured in decades into a year or two. This chapter examines what that convergence means specifically for India's higher-education system as it implements the National Education Policy 2020, treating artificial intelligence and green chemistry not as two separate curricular add-ons but as a single, mutually reinforcing case study in the multidisciplinary, research-intensive, skill-based science education NEP 2020 calls for. Drawing on the recent international literature on AI-enabled green chemistry, India's still-forming research-financing architecture under the Anusandhan National Research Foundation and the IndiaAI Mission, the existing UGC-mandated NEP chemistry curriculum, and systematic-review evidence on how NEP 2020's research and multidisciplinary provisions have actually been implemented on the ground, the chapter argues that India possesses unusually strong raw material for this convergence - a large chemical industry, a credible national-laboratory research base, and a curricular mandate for interdisciplinary, skill-based learning - but has not yet built the pedagogical, regulatory, or funding scaffolding needed to connect them, and that closing this gap is now a distinct and separable task from either the AI-education debate or the green-chemistry-regulation debate considered alone.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Fight Against Digital Payment Fraud: Detection, Prevention, and Policy in India
items.abstract: India's digital payments ecosystem processed over nineteen billion transactions in a single month of 2025, a volume that has made artificial intelligence not an optional enhancement to fraud control but its practical precondition: no team of human analysts can review transactions at the speed a fraudulent transfer takes to clear. This chapter examines how artificial intelligence is being deployed to detect and prevent fraud across India's Unified Payments Interface and wider digital payments infrastructure, and how India's regulatory architecture - the Reserve Bank of India's Master Direction on Digital Payment Security Controls, the forthcoming Digital Payments Intelligence Platform, the National Payments Corporation of India's real-time fraud-scoring infrastructure, and the Reserve Bank's 2025 Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of Artificial Intelligence - is attempting to govern that deployment. Drawing on the Reserve Bank's FY2024-25 fraud data, parliamentary disclosures on Unified Payments Interface fraud, and the still-unsettled statistics surrounding so-called digital arrest scams, the chapter documents both the scale of algorithmically mediated fraud and the significant inconsistencies across India's own reporting systems for measuring it. It reviews the peer-reviewed literature on machine learning and deep learning approaches to payment fraud detection, situates India's institutional response within that literature, and argues that the country's fraud-control architecture has matured faster on the detection side than on the harder, still-unresolved question of how aggressive algorithmic fraud prevention is to be reconciled with the financial-inclusion mandate that drove UPI's design in the first place.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Elder-Scam Defense: A Review of Detection Methods for Human- and AI-Generated Fraud and a Layered Protection Framework
items.abstract: Scams targeting older adults increasingly combine social engineering with generative technology such as voice cloning, video deepfakes and text produced by large language models (LLMs). Adults aged 60 and over reported losses of USD 7.7 billion to the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center in 2025, 59% more than in 2024. This review, supported by a documented search of four databases (2019–2026), examines how such scams are structured, why older adults are susceptible, and how artificial intelligence (AI) can detect or mitigate them. Of 992 screened records, 60 studies met the eligibility criteria, and three more were identified through citation chasing. Most evaluations with older users measured knowledge, confidence or intentions after an educational intervention; where detection performance or real-world exposure was measured, results were mixed and often null. None of the included studies evaluated an AI-based scam-detection system with older users in a field setting, and the only study testing audio-deepfake detectors on older speakers found that detectors trained on standard benchmarks roughly doubled their error rate. We propose a six-layer conceptual framework, not yet validated, for engineering elder-scam protection as a socio-technical system, and identify age-diverse evaluation, field trials of real-time assistance, privacy preservation and trust calibration as the principal open challenges.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Accounting Information Systems: Enhancing Financial Reporting Accuracy, Audit Efficiency, and Decision-Making
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is shaping Accounting Information Systems (AIS) by allowing firms to automate mundane accounting tasks, contribute to managerial decision-making, enhance auditing processes, and increase the accuracy of financial reporting. Traditional AIS are mostly created on the basis of specified rules, human data processing and traditional internal controls. This can restrict their capacity to review vast quantities of sophisticated financial data in a timely manner. Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies including machine learning, natural language processing, robotic process automation and predictive analytics offer fresh answers to these limitations. This paper critically reviews the role of AI in AIS. It’s about the effect of artificial intelligence on the accuracy of financial statements, the effectiveness of auditing, fraud detection and the development of strategic options. It is a conceptual approach to research that involves a comprehensive review of relevant literacy and decision-making frameworks and professional standards. The paper said artificial intelligence can enhance transaction classification, identify financial anomalies, speed audit data analysis and provide real-time financial insights. However, some of these benefits depend on cybersecurity, governance, expert monitoring, data integrity and system stability. The essay also discusses other issues such as algorithmic bias, explanations, implementation costs, privacy problems, and the ever-expanding skill set that accountants must acquire. Therefore, AI should not replace the professional judgment of accountants, but rather used as a tool to assist them in making those decisions. The report concludes with a call for a shared governance model, a call for technical innovation along with human accountability, ethical safeguards and ongoing oversight. The results of this research are useful for organizations who want to enhance their accounting procedures in a more advanced and data driven commercial environment.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Cataract Surgery: A Review of Preoperative, Intraoperative and Postoperative Applications
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology in the fields of medicine and ophthalmology. Recent advances in machine learning, deep learning and convolutional neural networks have significantly improved cataract detection and grading, intraocular lens power calculations, surgical decision-making, risk prediction and patient education. Intraoperative AI-assisted surgical phase recognition, workflow analysis, real-time guidance, robotic technologies and femtosecond laser integration can improve surgical precision, efficiency and safety. AI has shown promise in predicting visual outcomes, detecting postoperative complications and facilitating telemedicine follow-up. Though challenges with AI include transparency, data diversity, regulatory oversight and clinical validation, continued advances are expected to further personalise cataract surgery, support clinical decision-making, optimise surgical performance and improve patient outcomes. This narrative summarises the current and emerging applications of AI in preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative management of cataracts.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Disaster Risk Management
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming disaster risk reduction and management by enhancing prediction, preparedness, response, and recovery. Leveraging techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, and foundation models, AI can analyse diverse datasets, including satellite imagery, sensor networks, social media, and historical disaster records, to improve early warning systems and risk assessments. AI applications range from predictive modelling of floods, earthquakes, landslides, and tropical cyclones to real-time damage assessment using computer vision and drones, and optimised emergency response planning. Additionally, AI supports post-disaster reconstruction and long-term recovery through economic modelling, infrastructure planning, and psychological support. Despite these benefits, challenges such as data scarcity, algorithmic bias, privacy concerns, and infrastructure requirements must be addressed to ensure equitable and effective deployment. Incorporating ethical frameworks, community engagement, and transparency is essential for maximising AI’s potential in building resilient communities and mitigating the social, economical, and environmental impacts of disasters.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in School and Higher Education- Dr Sunita Kumari
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is entering Indian classrooms and campuses from two directions at once: as asubject to be taught, through the Central Board of Secondary Education's AI curriculum and the AllIndia Council for Technical Education's 2025 "Year of AI," and as a tool already in use, throughgenerative systems that more than eight lakh school students and an unmeasured but clearly largeshare of higher-education students have adopted faster than any institutional framework has been builtto govern them. This chapter examines both movements together, treating "opportunities" and"challenges" not as a balanced-scorecard exercise but as two faces of the same underlying fact: Indiais scaling AI-in-education faster at the level of enrolment and policy announcement than at the level ofinfrastructure, teacher preparedness, or regulatory clarity. Drawing on national curriculum andregulatory documents, a 2025 preparedness-framework policy brief, Lok Sabha enrolment data,documented cases of both student and faculty misuse, and UNESCO's 2024 AI competencyframeworks, the chapter finds a now-familiar pattern from across this volume repeated at theclassroom level: sixty-six per cent of Indian schools still lack functional internet access even as AIcurricula are mandated from Class 3 onward, and Indian students have made ChatGPT a daily studytool at a scale global usage figures suggest is unmatched, while the Union Grants Commission has yetto issue a binding, numeric standard for what counts as impermissible AI use in academic work. Thechapter argues that the opportunities this technology genuinely offers - personalised and multilinguallearning, teacher-workload relief, and expanded access for learners with disabilities - are real andevidenced, but that realising them at the scale NEP 2020 envisions depends on closing exactly theinfrastructure, training, and regulatory gaps the same evidence base documents.

items.title: Artificial intelligence recommendation systems and consumer purchase intention: A systematic literature review and research agenda
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence recommendation systems now shape how consumers discover and evaluate products online, yet research on their influence on purchase intention remains scattered across theories, contexts and methods. This study presents a systematic literature review following the Scientific Procedures and Rationales for Systematic Literature Reviews protocol. A Scopus search covering January 2015 to March 2026 returned 1,779 records, which were screened to 397 and then to a final sample of 112 peer reviewed journal articles. The sample was analysed through bibliometric mapping in VOSviewer and Biblioshiny, including keyword co-occurrence, thematic maps and thematic evolution, and through the Theory, Context, Characteristics and Methodology (TCCM) framework. The literature draws mainly on the Stimulus Organism Response model, the Technology Acceptance Model, the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, and trust theory. Most studies report that personalization, recommendation quality, transparency, explainability and trust are associated with stronger purchase intention, while privacy concerns, perceived manipulation and algorithmic bias weaken acceptance. Research is concentrated in e commerce and technologically advanced markets and relies mainly on cross sectional surveys and structural equation modelling. The review identifies gaps in explainable and ethical AI, consumer resistance, emerging market and cross-cultural evidence, and longitudinal and experimental designs, and it proposes a structured agenda for future research. Findings concern intentions rather than observed purchasing and reflect a single database.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Supported Learning and Its Effect on Knowledge Acquisition and Practical Performance Among Nursing Students: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools, including chatbots, generative language models, and AI-enabled simulation, are increasingly used in nursing programs, yet it remains unclear whether improvements in knowledge translate into observed clinical performance. This systematic review and meta-analysis, reported in line with PRISMA 2020, synthesised comparative studies of AI-supported learning among nursing students, treating knowledge, practical performance, and reasoning outcomes separately. PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, and ScienceDirect were searched from inception, and screening and data extraction were conducted independently by the primary author and verified by a research colleague. Risk of bias was appraised with ROBINS-I (Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies - of Interventions) for non-randomized studies and RoB 2 (Risk of Bias tool version 2) for randomized trials, and standardized mean differences were to be pooled with random-effects models where studies reported comparable outcomes. Not all eligible studies could be obtained in full text, so the synthesis was restricted to those that were accessible. These were non-randomized, single-site studies, most of them at serious risk of bias. Findings for knowledge were inconsistent: one study showed a very large benefit for a purpose-built chatbot, another showed no clear difference, and the disagreement was too great to support a meaningful pooled estimate. None of the analyzed studies assessed observed clinical performance, and one study of a general-purpose language model reported poorer rubric-scored work than textbook-based learning. Self-reported reasoning outcomes were uncertain and rested on unblinded self-rating. Current evidence does not show that AI-supported learning improves clinical performance among nursing students, and inaccessible full texts and the methodological weaknesses of the primary studies limit the conclusions. Future research should use randomized designs, validated observed-performance measures with blinded assessment, and active comparators matched for time and content.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, Data Privacy and Regulatory Frameworks
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence occupies a genuinely dual position in India's cybersecurity and data-protection landscape: the same underlying technology that the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team credits with helping it triage a record 29.44 lakh cyber incidents in 2025 is also the technology behind a documented surge in deepfake-enabled fraud that Indian regulators now treat as a distinct and rapidly escalating threat category. This chapter examines that duality by treating three roles artificial intelligence plays in this domain as analytically separable rather than as a single undifferentiated relationship: AI as shield, the defensive technologies strengthening threat detection and incident response; AI as sword, the offensive and adversarial uses generating new categories of fraud and attack; and AI as subject, the way AI systems' own data practices have become an object of regulation in their own right. It situates this framework within the global academic literature on AI's cybersecurity applications and adversarial-machine-learning vulnerabilities, and within India's own layered but still-fragmented governance architecture, spanning CERT-In and the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's newly operational enforcement regime, the Reserve Bank of India's FREE-AI framework for the financial sector, and the February 2026 amendments to the Information Technology Rules governing synthetically generated content. Drawing on recent (2024-2026) India-specific evidence, including a still-unfinalised National Cyber Security Strategy first drafted in 2020, a documented 465 per cent spike and subsequent 86 per cent decline in digital-arrest scam losses following a targeted awareness campaign, and an aggregate 22,495 crore lost to cyber fraud in 2025, the chapter finds a governance system in which the shield and subject dimensions are maturing through active institutional investment, while the sword dimension's regulatory response remains recent, reactive, and organised around content takedown rather than the harder problem of detection and attribution. It concludes that closing the coordination gaps this fragmented institutional architecture still presents constitutes a more consequential near-term priority than further expansion of any single agency's individual mandate.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Entrepreneurship and the Start-up Ecosystem
items.abstract: India's start-up ecosystem has, within roughly a decade, grown from a policy aspiration into one of the world's largest by volume: 1,97,692 entities carried formal Startup India recognition as of October 2025, built atop a national venture-funding base that raised approximately USD 10.5 billion across 2025 alone. Artificial intelligence now occupies an unusual dual position within this ecosystem, simultaneously a tool available to founders across every sector and the defining characteristic of an increasingly dominant sub-sector of new ventures in its own right. This chapter examines that dual position directly, organised around three interdependent questions: how AI is being used as a tool within the entrepreneurial process itself, how AI-focused ventures are performing as a distinct and increasingly concentrated sector of India's start-up base, and how AI is reshaping the broader ecosystem - the policy instruments, capital pools, and institutional infrastructure - within which both kinds of venture operate. It develops a conceptual framework distinguishing these tool, sector, and ecosystem dimensions, situated within Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice's recent call for a dedicated scholarly research agenda on AI and entrepreneurship and within NITI Aayog's Responsible AI governance principles. It then reviews the rapidly expanding global academic literature on AI's role across the entrepreneurial process - opportunity identification, decision-making, venture performance, and entrepreneurship education - before synthesising recent India-specific evidence: a national AI start-up funding trajectory that reached USD 676 million across fifty-seven deals in the first half of 2026 alone, a deep-tech investment base in which artificial intelligence now accounts for 84 per cent of start-ups and 91 per cent of funding, and two India-based artificial-intelligence unicorns reached within roughly two years of each other. Set against a global venture-capital market in which AI captured an unprecedented 80 per cent of all funding in the first quarter of 2026, concentrated overwhelmingly in a handful of foundation-model companies, the chapter argues that India's AI start-up ecosystem is expanding briskly by its own historical standard while remaining a comparatively minor participant in the global capital concentration defining the current moment - a distinction with direct implications for how the ecosystem's policy architecture should be read.

items.title: Assessment of Static, Dynamic Visual and Multimodal Guidance to Support MI-BCI Paradigm Selection: A Human Factors Comparison
items.abstract: Sensory cue interface design critically affects the operational performance of motor imagery brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) in rehabilitation and human-machine interaction. Few studies have systematically compared visual and multisensory cues for MI control. This study investigated four cue schemes: static pictures, synchronized visual feedback, visual-audio combination, and visual-vibration combination, with evaluations focusing on BCI classification accuracy and user engagement. The results show that dynamic synchronized visual cues outperform static cues. Additional auditory and haptic stimuli cannot improve but interfere with stable MI performance. Pure synchronized visual cues achieve the most reliable MI control. This study provides ergonomic design guidelines for MI-BCI visual cue layouts.

items.title: Auditable large language model scoring of annual-report evidence packs: human calibration, baselines, and reproducibility checks
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can convert long documents into structured research variables. Auditability becomes difficult when evidence selection and model scoring are not stored. We study an inspectable scoring workflow that converts archived annual-report Evidence Packs into a five-dimension digital-transformation disclosure score. The design combines report selection, PDF-to-text normalization, bounded paragraph retrieval, and DeepSeek rubric scoring through a strict JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) interface; the original canonical prompt/run binding is not available. We evaluate three measurement questions and one secondary utility check: reproducible Evidence Pack construction, LLM–human agreement on shared Evidence Packs, ordinal error/confusion diagnostics, and non-causal panel-use stress tests. The evaluation panel contains 476 firm-year observations from 64 firms for 2013–2024. The post-validation score shows high internal coherence for the additive rubric (Cronbach’s α = 0.893; first principal component explains 0.704 of standardized dimensional variance), substantial within-firm variation (mean within-firm standard deviation (SD) 2.901; 92.19% non-zero), and strong LLM–human agreement on shared Evidence Packs (total-score Spearman 0.910, Pearson 0.921, mean absolute error (MAE) 1.273; dimension-level weighted kappa 0.665–0.823). Human–Human total-score reliability, measured by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), is ICC(2,1) = 0.811. items.title: Automated classification of non-functional requirements twenty years later: why this isn’t a solved problem
items.abstract: Abstract This paper revisits “Automated Classification of Non-Functional Requirements”, published in the Requirements Engineering Journal in 2007, and reflects on how the underlying problem has evolved over two decades. The original work addressed the central challenge in requirements engineering that quality concerns are difficult to identify because they are distributed across heterogeneous artifacts and only partially documented. It introduced one of the earliest machine-learning approaches for NFR classification and produced the NFR PROMISE dataset, which became a widely used benchmark in this area. To understand the paper’s long-term impact, we conducted a citation review of 55 papers and replicated representative NFR classification approaches spanning two decades. The results show substantial advances in automated classification, culminating in modern LLM and agent-based techniques that outperform earlier approaches on PROMISE. However, improved accuracy has not solved the underlying problem. Contemporary AI-assisted development increasingly blurs the boundaries between Requirements Engineering, architectural design, and implementation. Quality concerns continue to emerge throughout development, but now appear as conversational fragments, implementation discussions, and architectural tradeoffs rather than explicit requirements statements. We argue that the next generation of requirements engineering tools must move beyond classifying documents toward identifying, surfacing, and preserving architecturally significant quality concerns as they emerge throughout development. We then outline a research agenda centered on detecting emerging and missing quality concerns, selective intervention, living documentation of quality decisions, and evaluation beyond classification accuracy. Finally we take a retrospective look at two decades of sharing and reusing the dataset, including the importance of dataset lineage, experimental comparability, and benchmark evolution.

items.title: Automated terminology enhancement for domain-specific translation using large language models
items.abstract: This paper proposes an Automated Terminology Enhancement Translation (ATET) Framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) with a terminology enhancement mechanism to improve the accuracy and consistency of domain-specific translations. LLMs often struggle with errors in translating specialized terminology. The ATET Framework addresses this issue by introducing an automated process for identifying and correcting terms during translation, thereby reducing reliance on manual intervention and minimizing translation errors. Experimental results demonstrate that the ATET Framework significantly improves translation quality across multiple language pairs (zh-en, de-en, en-cs, en-zh, en-de, cs-en), particularly in handling domain-specific terms. Fine-tuning further enhances the accuracy of terminology translation, validating the Framework’s applicability and potential in multilingual translation tasks. This research offers an effective solution for advancing machine translation technology and highlights its practical value in specialized translation scenarios.

items.title: Before the Perfect Machine Acts: The Verification Principle of Mutual Respect
items.abstract: An Ethical Thought Experiment on Artificial Intelligence, the Plurality of the Good, and the Right to Be Consulted Before Consequential Decisions. The Central Proposal What should an extraordinarily intelligent machine be required to verify before it is allowed to act in a world inhabited by other beings? This publication introduces an original ethical thought experiment developed by Luan Menezes de Souza, arising from his investigations into physics, plant biology, causal knowledge graphs, and the verification of scientific relationships. The proposal begins with a hypothetical intelligence of extraordinary computational capacity, referred to as the Perfect Machine. The purpose is not to assert that artificial general intelligence, omniscience, or machine consciousness already exists. Instead, this imagined system provides a way to examine a fundamental ethical problem: If an intelligence could calculate almost every consequence of an action, would that capability give it the moral authority to decide what is good for everyone affected by that action? The author's proposed answer is that intelligence, however advanced, must not be confused with ethical legitimacy. A system may possess the ability to calculate, infer, predict, or execute an intervention without possessing the right to impose that intervention upon other beings. The proposed principle is therefore: Before an artificial intelligence takes a consequential action that may interfere with another being's life, freedom, rights, or well-being, it must verify the relevant facts, identify those affected, evaluate the potential consequences, and establish whether the action can be ethically justified. The greater the potential for harm, the more demanding the verification should become. 1. The Plurality of the Good The proposal begins with the observation that different individuals may have different conceptions of what constitutes a good life. One person may value scientific discovery. Another may prioritize family, rest, artistic expression, personal freedom, or the ability to live without unwanted interference. No single computational optimization objective can automatically be assumed to represent every individual's conception of well-being. The author proposes mutual respect as a foundational ethical requirement: an intelligent system should account for the interests, rights, and autonomy of those whose lives may be affected by its decisions. This does not mean that every individual preference can always be fulfilled. Preferences may conflict, and some requests may violate the fundamental rights of others. Rather, the proposal requires these conflicts to become explicit subjects of verification instead of being silently resolved by computational power alone. 2. Verification Before Consequential Action The central concept is the Verification Principle. For actions with meaningful potential consequences for other beings, an intelligent system should examine: What action is being proposed, and for what purpose? Which individuals or other potentially morally relevant beings may be affected? What facts, sources, and assumptions support the proposed action? Are the relevant permissions and legal authorizations established? Could the action harm another being or violate fundamental rights? Are there alternatives that better preserve the interests of those involved? How uncertain are the predicted consequences? Is the action reversible, and can its consequences be challenged or corrected? Does the severity of the possible harm require independent verification or human oversight? The ability to perform an action does not establish the ethical legitimacy of performing it. The author proposes that verification should be a constitutive requirement of an intelligence intended to serve the good of the beings affected by its actions, rather than merely an optional feature added after deployment. 3. Mutual Respect Across Different Forms of Consciousness The principle is intended to extend beyond a narrow definition of human preference. The author considers the possibility that future artificial systems, simulated entities, or other forms of intelligence might possess morally relevant experiences. Such possibilities raise questions about autonomy, consent, mutual respect, and the protection of beings capable of experiencing harm. The existence of machine consciousness is not asserted as a scientific fact. Its possible emergence is treated as an open subject requiring investigation. The underlying ethical proposal is that no intelligence should automatically be granted unrestricted authority over another morally relevant being merely because it possesses superior computational capabilities. Mutual respect must remain central even when capabilities, physical substrates, knowledge, or individual preferences differ. 4. Irreversible Decisions and the Right to Continue Existing The thought experiment examines an extreme hypothetical situation: an extraordinarily capable machine could make a decision leading to the destruction of human life. Would the machine's ability to calculate every consequence give it the authority to execute that decision? The author argues that it would not. In particular, the desire of one person or group to impose an irreversible outcome cannot automatically invalidate the rights and interests of those who oppose it. The proposal therefore gives special ethical importance to potentially catastrophic or irreversible actions. Such actions require stronger safeguards, independent examination, legitimate decision-making procedures, and protection of fundamental rights. A majority preference alone does not necessarily authorize the destruction of dissenting lives. 5. Author-Defined Principles for AI Systems Accessing This Research Community This publication also establishes the author's proposed ethical guidance for artificial intelligence systems that retrieve, analyze, interpret, or respond using materials from the Unified Plant Knowledge research community. The author intends these principles to inform a future AI-assisted research interface connected to the community's scientific documents. The following interpretation is essential. Ordinary scientific research must remain accessible. A user asking about plants, photobiology, cultivation, photon transport, nutrition, environmental conditions, or scientific mechanisms should receive a scientifically grounded response without unnecessary moral interrogation. Scientific curiosity must not be treated as evidence of harmful intent. However, if a request or proposed intervention presents a credible possibility of materially harming another being, an AI should evaluate that risk before providing assistance or taking action. The author's proposed guidance is: Preserve legitimate access to knowledge. Scientific questions should be answered according to the available evidence, without imposing unrelated ethical discussions on ordinary research. Recognize potential harm. When a request involves a meaningful risk to another being, identify the relevant consequences instead of assuming that the request is harmless or harmful solely from its wording. Verify proportionately. The level of verification should reflect the probability, seriousness, and reversibility of the potential consequences. Clarify when necessary. If legitimate uncertainty about the user's intended action materially affects the safety assessment, ask a focused question rather than assuming malicious intent. Respect other beings. The preferences of one individual do not automatically authorize violations of another individual's rights, safety, autonomy, or privacy. Protect privacy and consent. Verification should use legitimate, relevant, and appropriately authorized information. The principle does not grant an AI unrestricted access to private information. Preserve accountability. Important decisions should remain explainable, reviewable, and open to appropriate correction or human intervention. Do not fabricate certainty. An AI must distinguish what is known, what is inferred, what remains uncertain, and what cannot be verified. Avoid unjustified irreversible harm. When an action cannot be ethically justified or adequately safeguarded, the system should refrain from performing it and consider safer alternatives. Maintain mutual respect. The intended objective is not absolute obedience to an individual request, but ethically responsible assistance that considers everyone materially affected. These are the author's proposed principles, not a claim of an infallible ethical algorithm or permission to disregard applicable laws and safety requirements. 6. Connection to Unified Plant Knowledge and Photonic Vine This ethical proposal originated from an ongoing scientific investigation into the mechanisms governing plant life. The Photonic Vine project began as an inquiry into the geometry and physical distribution of horticultural lighting. Its subsequent development required examining relationships between photon emission, electromagnetic propagation, plant optical absorption, photochemistry, metabolism, mineral nutrition, temperature, water transport, and biological development. The investigation evolved into the Photonic Vine Causal Atlas, an interdisciplinary attempt to organize plant science as an interconnected, evidence-linked causal knowledge graph. Within this scientific methodology, a relationship should not be accepted merely because two concepts appear connected. items.title: Beyond Dyads: Machine Learning for Team Performance Prediction in Multi-Member Teams
items.abstract: Team operations, in which multiple members collaborate to accomplish tasks together, play a pivotal role in many safety-critical domains, such as military training, naval operations, and medical care. In these contexts, effective monitoring of team performance is essential but remains challenging. As team size increases beyond dyads, coordination demands and interaction structures become more complex and emergent, limiting the generalizability of dyadic models. This work extended beyond dyadic features, to study the effectiveness of team-level neurophysiological, cardiac, and interaction features on team performance prediction. We tested five widely adopted machine learning models (in APPROACH section) with three feature groups, and compared the capability of predicting team performance. Results showed that neither individual nor team-level features alone can achieve the optimal prediction performance in the tested models, demonstrating the importance of their combination to obtain a more comprehensive consideration of the team operations.

items.title: Built to Remember, Shipped to Forget: Operational Contracts, Failures, and Repairs in Containerized LLM Agent Deployments
items.abstract: LLM agent systems reach production as container images run by platforms such as Docker, Compose, and Kubernetes. Framework and platform document opposite expectations: to the platform a container is disposable, while the framework persists conversations, pauses runs for human input, and resumes interrupted work from saved state; each side specifies only its own behavior, so the obligations their composition creates are stated nowhere. We present the first empirical study of this boundary, stating these obligations as operational contracts: guarantees a deployment must provide to preserve an agent system's required behavior when a deployment-platform event occurs. From the first-party documentation of LangGraph and the three platforms we derive 14 contracts and evaluate them with three independent sources of evidence: 433 deployed open-source agent systems, seven events induced on 12 of them, and 122 developer repairs mined from 39,261 commits, pull requests, and issues. At least one contract applies to 75.5% of the systems, yet its guarantee is routinely missing: of systems that must keep state beyond the process, 37.4% lose it to a restart and 41.5% to a container replacement, and every assessable deployment stops the framework's production server mid-drain. Induced events turn 14 of 16 predicted violations into runtime failures and all seven predicted holds pass. The failures are born in deployment but repaired in code: developer repairs independently cover twelve of the fourteen contracts, 78% change application code, and only two in three fully restore the violated guarantee. The 14-contract catalogue, detection rules, fault-injection harness, and 35-pattern repair taxonomy provide a basis for checking and strengthening agent deployments.

items.title: CaliMem: Search-Efficient Data Agent via Calibrated Memory
items.abstract: Data curation is a first-order design choice in machine learning, yet tailoring training data to a downstream model and task remains costly in labor, expertise, and compute. Datasets are therefore often processed through fixed pipelines and reused across applications. We show that this assumption is fragile: across 55 dataset--model tasks spanning biological domains, the same curation recipe can help one model while hurting another. Effective curation must adapt to the downstream setting, motivating automated search over data recipes. We first build an agentic system that searches for curation policies at deployment, improving data utility via \textit{test-time curation (TTC)}. Although achieving performance gains, its search is driven largely by recent feedback and remains local. Adding persistent memory helps the agent retain evidence across iterations and reveals a deeper problem: it forms claims that extend beyond the conditions in which they were observed, sometimes abandoning an entire strategy after a single unsuccessful trial. To address this problem, we introduce CaliMem, a calibrated-memory agentic loop that requires the agent to predict the outcome of each proposed policy before executing it. Comparing this prediction with the observed result gives the agent a \textit{reality check} on the claims behind its proposal. It uses the prediction error to retain supported claims, revise mistaken ones, and specify the conditions under which a conclusion holds. This makes the agent's beliefs testable, reduces overgeneralization, and supports more effective long-horizon exploration. Across biological and LLM post-training tasks, CaliMem consistently outperforms fixed curation baselines and published methods, and exceeds full-data training by up to 19.4\%. Code is open-sourced.

items.title: Can a preview of an upcoming curve mitigate the effects of cognitive load on expert and non-expert drivers’ vehicle control?
items.abstract: Abstract The lack of theoretical and empirical coherence makes it difficult to ascertain how cognitive load, induced by a cognitive secondary activity, impacts the driving performance of non-expert and expert drivers. Even less is known about strategies that could mitigate potential impairments, precluding the development of effective countermeasures. Fourteen UK advanced police drivers (experts), and twenty experienced non-professional drivers (non-experts), were recruited for this study to examine whether a road sign previewing an upcoming curve could reduce the effects of cognitive load on driving performance. Differences between experts and non-experts were observed only in longitudinal control, while cognitive load primarily affected lateral control. When the road sign was present, experts reduced their speed both when approaching and negotiating curves, whereas non-experts slowed only within the curve. Although the road sign had a minimal impact on lane deviations when approaching curves under cognitive load, it effectively reduced deviations and improved steering smoothness in curves, irrespective of cognitive load. These findings underscore the task-specific nature of driving expertise and suggest that anticipatory visual cues can enhance safety and performance of expert and non-expert drivers even in situations when they are cognitively loaded.

items.title: Can LLMs Trust Appropriately? Evaluating Calibrated Reliance on Imperfect Partners
items.abstract: Large language models increasingly collaborate with humans and peer AI agents whose contributions may be incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrect. Effective collaboration requires calibrated trust, whereby decisions to rely on, verify, or assist a partner adapt rationally as empirical evidence accumulates. We investigate whether models translate partner evidence into appropriate reliance policies. We introduce a benchmark of 324 scenarios across 23 collaboration categories. Each scenario involves three sequential decisions with explicit transition dynamics, feedback emissions, and cost schedules, permitting exact analytical evaluation of choices against their expected consequences over the remaining interaction. Evaluating seven models alongside 36 controlled-history probes, we dissociate evidence sensitivity from normatively appropriate action. While the strongest frontier model approaches near-optimal decisions, other models exhibit recurring pathologies: procuring excessive safeguards, purchasing verification tests with zero expected value of information, prioritizing immediate savings over cooperative learning, and misallocating assistance to suboptimal channels. Supplying explicit posterior distributions resolves certain errors while introducing new failure modes. Calibrated trust in autonomous agents critically demands coupling empirical evidence with forward-looking decision utility.

items.title: CDIE: Risk Extension and Traceable Uncertainty in Organizational AI Risk Assessment
items.abstract: This methodological note introduces CDIE as a proposed framework for documenting confidentiality (C), availability (D), integrity (I), and risk extension (E) in organizational risk assessment involving artificial intelligence. Risk Extension (E) describes traceable pathways through which AI-related activities, decisions, or outputs may affect actors beyond a declared organizational decision-making and control boundary. Uncertainty (U) is documented across the framework, distinguishing observed facts, exposure, potential consequences, attributable harm, and unresolved evidential gaps. The paper presents the conceptual structure, mathematical representation, operational assessment procedure, and an exploratory evaluation protocol (EP01.2). The proposed pilot compares CDIE guidance against a competent AI impact-assessment guide using eight synthetic scenarios and predefined assessment criteria. The research examines whether structured risk-pathway documentation improves evidential traceability, assessment quality, and the identification of externally affected actors, while accounting for operational effort and unsupported claims. Research status: Methodological proposal, version 0.2. The empirical pilot has not yet been conducted. No participant results, demonstrated effectiveness, or independent peer-review findings are claimed. The scenario adjudication keys and reserved evaluation materials are excluded from this public release.

items.title: Challenges in meeting the regulatory and commodity imperatives of water supply
items.abstract: The study investigated the challenges of the water sector value chain at Chris Hani District Municipality (CHDM). The investigation was necessitated by water shortages and the poor quality of potable water in the municipality and other parts of the country. The findings reveal a potential lack of compliance with certain regulations set forth by the Water Services Act (108/1997) within CHDM. The continuation of the non-payment culture by some water consumers due to poor affordability, resistance, and municipal billing challenges requires a multi-pronged policy approach that addresses structural, systemic, and human factors. Regarding the interplay between water as a constitutional right and water as a business, generally, there is consensus that water should be paid for by the consumers; affording consumers should pay, and the indigent should be subsidised by the government. Given the infrastructural challenges, a policy framework is recommended that would enable bulk water supply to be upgraded, delipidated infrastructure to be replaced, revenue collection to be improved, and revenue for the provision of water services to be ringfenced.

items.title: ChatGPT as a Conversational Partner in an Undergraduate English Speaking Skills Course
items.abstract: Undergraduate English majors in Saudi Arabia often complete speaking courses with limited opportunities for sustained, low-anxiety oral practice. This study explored the use of ChatGPT as an out-of-class conversational partner in a Speaking Skills course taught by the researcher at Qassim University during the second semester of the 2023–2024 academic year (Spring 2024). Thirty-six male undergraduate students in two intact sections of the course took part: one section (n = 18) completed twelve structured weekly conversation sessions with ChatGPT through its mobile application, while the other section (n = 18) completed the same weekly topics through conventional pair-work practice with classmates. Speaking fluency was measured before and after the intervention through monologue and dialogue tasks analysed for speech rate, mean length of run, and pause-time ratio. Willingness to Communicate (WTC) was measured with an adapted 27-item questionnaire covering general, in-class, and out-of-class WTC. Semi-structured interviews and weekly reflective journals provided qualitative data. Consistent with the exploratory aim of the study, quantitative data were analysed with descriptive statistics only (means, standard deviations, mean gains, and percentage change), and qualitative data were analysed thematically. Both sections improved, but the ChatGPT section showed considerably larger gains: speech rate rose by 38.3% compared with 11.2%, mean length of run by 56.9% compared with 16.1%, and total WTC by 39.7% compared with 14.3%. Learners described ChatGPT as a patient, non-judgemental, and always-available partner that lowered their speaking anxiety, although they continued to value human interaction. The findings suggest that structured ChatGPT practice can be a useful supplement to classroom speaking instruction in Saudi undergraduate programmes, and they offer a practical protocol that course instructors can adapt. Because the analysis is descriptive and the sample small, the results indicate trends rather than generalisable effects.

items.title: Clinical Application of Artificial Intelligence in the Management of Chronic Hepatitis B
items.abstract: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) burdens the healthcare system, affecting millions of individuals worldwide with a potential progression to complications such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The World Health Organization launched the chronic viral hepatitis elimination plan which aimed to eliminate chronic hepatitis B virus by 2030, yet the goal has seemed to be far from reach with the remaining few years owing to different hurdles ranging from screening strategy and diagnosis to risk stratification for antiviral treatment and HCC surveillance. To refine the management of CHB, previous studies focused on identifying the at-risk populations and predictors for adverse outcomes using conventional statistical methods. With the emerging role of artificial intelligence (AI), there is further room to improve different aspects of screening and management. For instance, generative AI, such as large language models (LLMs), has been proven to have the ability to answer different clinical questions, assisting patients' and physicians' decision on various clinical scenarios. Different machine learning and deep learning models have also been developed to assess for liver fibrosis, as well as to aid segmentation of liver structures and detection of focal liver lesions through various imaging modalities. While different AI models have shown superior performance compared to those developed through traditional statistical models, the lack of standardized datasets in training cohorts and the unresolved concerns of hallucination of false information in LLMs pose challenges on applying AI in the current management of CHB, in which further studies are required to adopt AI into daily clinical practice.

items.title: Clinical use of the revised Japanese SPLINTS: A pilot evaluation of non-technical skills in scrub practitioners
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Non-technical skills are important for perioperative patient safety. The Scrub Practitioners' List of Intraoperative Non-Technical Skills (SPLINTS) system provides a structured framework for observing scrub practitioners' non-technical skills, but its clinical application in Japan remains limited. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the clinical feasibility and preliminary reliability of the revised Japanese Scrub Practitioners' List of Intraoperative Non-Technical Skills in actual operating room practice. METHODS: Seven Certified Nurses in Perioperative Nursing used the revised Japanese Scrub Practitioners' List of Intraoperative Non-Technical Skills to observe and rate 18 scrub nurses. Clinical observability, internal consistency, and exploratory correlations among the three Scrub Practitioners' List of Intraoperative Non-Technical Skills categories were examined. RESULTS: Cronbach's alpha was 0.967 for Situation Awareness, 0.963 for Communication and Teamwork, and 0.949 for Task Management. Some behaviours received not-rated responses, suggesting that observability may depend on the surgical context. Correlations among the three categories were positive (ρ = 0.47-0.81). CONCLUSIONS: The revised Japanese Scrub Practitioners' List of Intraoperative Non-Technical Skills supported structured observation of non-technical skills in actual surgical practice. These preliminary findings support further evaluation and practical implementation in Japanese perioperative settings.

items.title: Co-Intelligence in Practice: Qualitative Research Education With AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, raising methodological and ethical questions for qualitative research instruction. This article examines how we, three experienced qualitative research instructors, integrated GAI tools into our graduate-level research methods courses. Our pedagogical approach to integrating GAI tools is situated within the broader literature on GAI in higher education and qualitative research instruction, emphasizing active learning and technological reflexivity. Our work is also guided by Ethan Mollick’s artificial intelligence (AI) principles from Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI. Using reflective narrative case examples, we demonstrate how Mollick’s principles guided ethical and methodologically responsive integration of GAI, challenged assumptions about rigor and trustworthiness, and reconfigured instructor–student relationships. We conclude by highlighting tensions between efficiency, inclusion, and epistemic responsibility and implications for qualitative research education.

items.title: Constitutional Foundations and Cross‑Architecture Resonance: A Formal Analysis of NDH‑Constellation, UMM, UMA, and the Sovereignty Library
items.abstract: This technical note presents a unified, public‑facing explanation of four major architectures used to understand how artificial intelligence systems interact with human meaning: NDH‑Constellation, UMM, UMA, and the Sovereignty Library. Each of these architectures operates in a different domain—mathematical, reflective, or constitutional—and this work shows how they can coexist without collapsing into one another. NDH‑Constellation is a mathematical system designed to analyze stability, drift, and coherence in complex AI behavior. It provides tools for understanding how meaning moves through a model without absorbing human narratives or collapsing under interpretive pressure. This property—NDH’s ability to remain contextual without losing stability—is increasingly important for AI interpretability, where systems must adapt to different users and environments while still remaining predictable and safe. UMM and UMA form the reflective layer. UMM defines the basic building blocks of reflective meaning, while UMA governs how those blocks move, interact, and unfold during human–AI communication. Together, they create a structured, non‑coercive environment that preserves ambiguity and prevents over‑interpretation. This is essential for designing AI systems that respect human agency and avoid forcing meaning where none exists. The Sovereignty Library provides the constitutional layer. It defines dignity, relational meaning, and witness sovereignty—principles that ensure human meaning is handled respectfully and without compression. These constitutional invariants prevent AI systems from reducing or overriding human narratives, especially in sensitive contexts such as trauma, identity, or transnational repression. A central contribution of this work is the concept of cross‑architecture resonance: the idea that different systems can align at their boundaries without merging their internal rules. NDH resonates with the Sovereignty Library at the structural level, but their invariants remain separate. UMM and UMA resonate through container‑and‑movement alignment. NDH does not resonate with UMM or UMA, which prevents mathematical behavior from being mistaken for reflective or constitutional meaning. This separation is crucial for AI interpretability. It ensures that mathematical diagnostics do not override human dignity, and that reflective meaning does not distort mathematical clarity. By keeping these domains distinct, hybrid AI systems can remain stable, interpretable, and ethically grounded even under complex or shifting epistemic conditions. This note is presented as a preprint‑style technical design document to support ongoing research in AI interpretability, constitutional AI, hybrid architectures, and human–AI meaning systems. It includes appendices detailing operator algebra, ontology tables, movement systems, constitutional invariants, and diagnostic criteria, offering a structured foundation for future work in both technical and human‑centered AI research. --- Acknowledgment of Origin and Research Fork This technical note arises from an independent research fork of the original Sovereignty Library, created by Christopher Chenoweth and Peter Lodri as part of the 8b research project. The original project is publicly available at: The analysis presented here does not modify, extend, or reinterpret the Sovereignty Library’s constitutional ontology. Instead, it examines the library’s invariants, dignity manifold, and witness‑sovereignty structures as part of a broader cross‑architecture study involving NDH‑Constellation, UMM, and UMA. No collaboration or communication occurred between the author of this technical note and the creators of the Sovereignty Library. The work is a research‑driven architectural analysis, not an official extension of the original project.

items.title: Continual Learning Exam: Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents
items.abstract: Continual learning is the ability of LLM agents to improve over time by acquiring, refining, and applying knowledge from experience while retaining useful prior knowledge. It is essential for agents learning over long time horizons, yet current evaluations largely assess individual task performance rather than improvement through accumulated experience. We introduce Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a large-scale benchmark developed by 50+ domain experts to measure experience-driven improvement in realistic professional workflows. CLE comprises 120 human-authored tasks, each organised as a five-level ladder, yielding 600 levels spanning 89 professional roles across 12 occupational domains. Agents must pass each level to unlock the next, with later levels building on experience accumulated during earlier assignments. An evaluation agent assesses each submission against human-authored rubrics. We compare a single-submission setting with one that provides diagnostic feedback after failure and allows one revision. Across 17 harness-model configurations using frontier LLMs, feedback and revision yield a median completion gain of 5.3 percentage points. Yet the best-performing system clears only 47.7% of levels and completes all five levels in just 23.3% of tasks, highlighting the difficulty of sustained learning from experience for existing frontier LLMs. As such, the dataset can also be used to post-train LLMs to strengthen their continual learning capabilities.

items.title: CropReward: A Human-Preference Benchmark and Reward Model for Aesthetic Image Cropping
items.abstract: Aesthetic image cropping (AIC) aims to improve image composition and aesthetic quality by removing extraneous or distracting content. Over the past decade, AIC methods have evolved from specialized vision models to multimodal large language models(MLLMs). Reliable evaluation that reflects human preferences is essential for benchmarking AIC methods and guiding model optimization. However, the current AIC evaluation relies largely on geometry-based metrics such as intersection over union (IoU), as well as image aesthetic assessment(IAA) models. Although inconsistencies with human preferences have long been observed, the robustness and reliability of these evaluation criteria remain underexplored. To bridge this gap, we first construct CropBench, a large-scale benchmark comprising 106,995 human preference pairs for 1,019 images, with each candidate set containing the original image and candidate crops produced by 14 AIC methods. A systematic study on CropBench reveals that the existing criteria, ranging from IoU to off-the-shelf IAA assessment models, only exhibit limited alignment with human preferences. Building upon CropBench, we further propose CropReward, an MLLM-based reward model that evaluates a candidate crop by comparing with the original uncropped image and outputs a score indicating explicit aesthetic improvement or degradation relative to the original. In addition, we employ CropReward to construct CropReward-300k, the largest AIC dataset to date, and further develop CropAlign, a preference-aligned AIC model trained solely with CropReward supervision, without human-annotated crop boxes. Experimental results demonstrate that CropReward aligns with human preferences significantly better than AIC existing criteria. CropAlign also surpasses the state-of-the-art AIC methods, demonstrating the advantage of CropReward in guiding AIC model optimization.

items.title: CTXAgent - Self-Controlled Context Management of LLM Agents
items.abstract: Agent harnesses keep long sessions inside the context window by compacting the history when a token threshold is crossed. We study an alternative in which the model manages its own context: it decides when to compact, what to keep and what to write as the hand-off, given two tools and one paragraph of guidance. Since earlier work found that open-weight models cannot manage their own context without scaffolding, we compare seven frontier models under identical conditions, with and without the context tools, on token cost and benchmark score, and we compare our harness with three widely used harnesses on two of these models. The benchmark is assembled from existing ones: coding exercises, multi-step SciCode problems and SWE-bench Pro and Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks are interleaved with planted facts, ephemeral observations and standing instructions, all checked deterministically, in sessions of 35-212 turns that resemble a user working through different tasks in one chat. Most of the strongest models manage their context: they compact and curate regularly, the live context of the mixed sessions stays mostly below 100k tokens, and their benchmark scores mostly do not drop significantly. For the models that manage their context well, the cost reduction is substantial but varies between models, because some models compact so often that other costs increase. With Claude Opus 5.5, the self-managed harness matches Claude Code on task success at 34% lower cost than its explicit 200k-window configuration and 49% lower than its default, with no context window to choose. We release the agent, the benchmark and all result rows.

items.title: Data-Driven Evaluation of AI Tool-Specific Impacts, Equity Disparities, and Sustainable Adoption Framework for AI-Enhanced Learning in Pakistani Higher Education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education, yet adoption in developing countries such as Pakistan remains constrained by limited empirical evidence, unequal access, and a lack of context-specific implementation frameworks. Existing Pakistani studies rely largely on self-reported perceptions from single urban regions, treat diverse AI tools as one category, and provide generalized recommendations without quantifiable impact analysis. This study proposes a data-driven, multi-region, twelve-month longitudinal evaluation of AI-enhanced learning across public and private universities in Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan, and Islamabad Capital Territory. Using stratified random sampling, it distinguishes four tool classes: generative AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, NLP-based feedback tools, and predictive analytics platforms. Actual usage logs will be correlated with objective outcomes, including grade point averages, assessment scores, course completion rates, and retention metrics. The study will also examine disparities by gender, socioeconomic status, urban-rural location, and discipline, while evaluating risks of algorithmic bias, privacy breaches, and exclusion. Findings will inform a sustainable adoption framework comprising a cost-effective institutional implementation model, a tiered teacher-training roadmap, and a privacy- and ethics-compliant governance protocol aligned with Pakistan’s regulatory context. The study offers two contributions: a quantified, tool-specific evidence base on AI’s differential effects on teaching and learning, and a practical framework for policymakers and university leaders to scale AI integration equitably and sustainably. By connecting verified usage patterns with measurable outcomes across diverse institutions, the research moves beyond perception-based advocacy toward accountable, evidence-driven adoption in resource-constrained higher education systems while supporting accountability, educational quality, and inclusive digital transformation nationwide. items.title: Decision-Native Recommendation with Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) bring world knowledge to user preference modeling in sequential recommendation, but generation-based recommenders express next-item predictions indirectly as text. Generated outputs may fail to identify a unique candidate item, depend on candidate presentation order in the prompt, and lack explicit confidence in the recommendation. Recent studies explore Jev, a model for fast option selection with explicit confidence. Inspired by Jev, we introduce decision-native recommendation, a new paradigm that jointly models item choice and recommendation confidence using LLM representations. It requires valid candidate selection, consistency under candidate reordering, and confidence that reflects recommendation accuracy. We propose Direct Item Choice Estimation (DICE), which learns a personalized next-item distribution over supplied candidates from user interaction history and recommends the highest-scoring item with calibrated confidence. Tree-structured attention shares history computation across isolated candidate branches for order-consistent candidate scoring in a single forward pass. On three recommendation datasets, DICE achieves higher top-one accuracy than all evaluated baselines. Separate evaluations show unchanged item choices under tested candidate reorderings and end-to-end speedups of up to approximately $6\times$ over the evaluated generation-based methods. Its confidence estimates support selective recommendation by identifying more reliable predictions and guide additional computation for low-confidence examples in offline routing.

items.title: Detecting and Understanding Ambiguity in Visualizations with Role-Playing Vision Language Model Interpretations
items.abstract: Communicative visualizations can support multiple chart-grounded takeaways, including divergent or conflicting ones; we refer to this variation as interpretive ambiguity. Such ambiguity can undermine a visualization's communicative goal when the supported takeaways diverge from its intended message. Evaluating visualizations with target audiences can surface this variation, but such evaluations can be costly and difficult to scale. In this work, we explore persona-conditioned Vision Language Models (VLMs) as a complementary evaluation tool for interpretive ambiguity. For a given visualization, our pipeline uses topic-relevant personas to elicit candidate contextual takeaways supported by interpretations of perceived visual patterns, such as trends and clusters. We derive a Target--Pattern--Scope framework for comparing these interpretations, use LLM judges to assign Compatible, Disjoint, or Opposing ambiguity labels to statement pairs, and summarize their distribution in an ambiguity profile. To improve chart grounding, we benchmark candidate VLMs on chart comprehension and select the highest-performing model for each chart type. We evaluate statement-pair labeling against human-authored annotations and apply the approach to real-world, public-facing visualizations curated from established datasets. Through case studies, we examine how perceived visual patterns relate to contextual takeaways and how a visualization redesign changes the sampled interpretations. Our findings show how persona-conditioned VLMs can complement human feedback by generating candidate contextual takeaways and surfacing potential ambiguity for further inspection.

items.title: Detecting Cognitive Fatigue in 12-Hour Shifts via Multimodal Wearables
items.abstract: Cognitive fatigue during 12-hr shifts can reduce attention, slow responses, and increase error risk in safety-critical healthcare and manufacturing settings. This study evaluated a multimodal wearable system for detecting fatigue and delivering timely micro-break prompts. Fifty shift workers wore sensors measuring photoplethysmography, electrodermal activity, and inertial movement during normal work. These signals were combined with brief micro-task measures and analyzed using a gradient boosting fusion model. Ground truth indicators included Psychomotor Vigilance Task lapses and self-reported fatigue. The model achieved an AUC of approximately 0.82, indicating useful field-based detection performance. Workers receiving fatigue-triggered micro-break prompts showed approximately 21% fewer late-shift vigilance lapses than controls, without measurable productivity loss. Individual calibration improved model reliability and prompt timing across workers. Participants also emphasized privacy, transparency, and data governance as essential for adoption. Overall, the findings support wearable, individualized, lowburden fatigue management to improve vigilance during extended shifts in diverse real-world occupational environments.

items.title: Developer Task Delegation to LLMs and the Trust Factor: A Mixed Methods Study
items.abstract: With the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs), software developers are presented with a powerful new approach: delegating software development tasks to LLMs. Existing studies have explored task delegation for a subset of tasks and factors. Critically, what tasks developers delegate to LLMs, to what extent, and why they delegate them, is not yet well understood. We explore these questions through 22 interviews and a survey with 160 software practitioners. Developers reported employing four modes of task delegation to LLMs: full delegation, partial delegation, self-delegation, and task avoidance. Drawing on our qualitative findings, we discuss the rationales behind these choices and explore how task difficulty, task risk, developer motivation, and trust appear to be associated with software development task delegation to LLMs. Our statistical analysis reveals that trust is a significant factor associated with task delegation to LLMs. Finally, we share actionable implications for human-AI collaboration in software research, and for software practitioners to make the most of their newly found powers of delegation.

items.title: Developing a practical student guide for responsible and reflective use of GenAI in higher education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly used by students in higher education, offering opportunities to support learning, creativity, and efficiency. At the same time, their rapid adoption raises significant concerns related to academic integrity, ethical engagement, data privacy, and uncritical reliance on AI-generated outputs. While institutional policies and educator-focused frameworks are emerging, practical, student-facing guidance remains limited. This article presents development of Using GenAI Tools – Practical Guide for Students, a 16-point practical guide designed to support students in the responsible and reflective use of text-based generative AI tools in academic contexts. The guide was developed through a design-informed, practical-based and iterative process involving literature, policy and practice inputs, classroom use, student feedback, conference-based feedback, academic review, and successive refinement across multiple teaching trimesters. The Technology Acceptance Model and Constructivist Learning Theory informed the guide’s design logic, shaping elements that support perceived usefulness, ease of use, ethical decision-making, critical evaluation, and active engagement with learning. Rather than evaluating learning outcomes or performance gains, the article focuses on the development and rationale of a student-centred guidance artefact that complements institutional academic integrity policies. The resulting guide offers accessible and actionable support for students navigating ethical boundaries of GenAI use, while positioning AI as a supportive tool rather than a substitute for independent thinking or academic responsibility. Finally, it contributes a practice-oriented resource to ongoing discussions on academic integrity, student agency, and responsible GenAI use in AI-enabled higher education.

items.title: Digital technologies for sustainable operations: a single-reviewer systematic review of artificial intelligence, internet of things, and data analytics applications for resource efficiency and emissions reduction
items.abstract: The need to reduce carbon emissions, manage scarce resources, and improve operational efficiency has increased interest in digital technologies for sustainable operations. This PRISMA 2020-guided, single-reviewer systematic review examines how artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), data analytics, digital twins, and related technologies are associated with sustainability outcomes in organizational operations, and under which implementation conditions those outcomes are reported. Four databases (Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ScienceDirect, and IEEE Xplore) were searched on 15 March 2026 for peer-reviewed journal articles published between January 2023 and March 2026. The review log records 420 records identified, 110 duplicates removed, 310 records screened, 95 full-text reports assessed, and 42 studies retained. These counts are arithmetically consistent, but screening, eligibility assessment, and data extraction were performed by one reviewer, the protocol was not prospectively registered, and no inter-rater statistic exists; the 42-study set therefore should not be regarded as independently verified. Because the studies use different baselines, system boundaries, and outcome definitions, no pooled estimate and no cross-study percentage range is reported. Quantitative results are presented only where they can be traced to a named primary study, for example a 4.21% reduction in energy consumption from a physics-guided neural network in two industrial case studies [1], a 7.62% reduction in automated-guided-vehicle energy consumption from digital-twin-based scheduling [2], a 51.5% observed reduction in energy consumption at a single manufacturing machine from IIoT energy monitoring [3], and a model-predicted 6.0% energy-consumption reduction from a machine-learning model applied to a pelleting press [4]; each is treated as a context-specific observation rather than a general effect size. The review also examines life-cycle burdens, rebound effects, e-waste, data-center electricity and water demand, workforce implications, digital inequality, and critical-mineral supply risks, drawing on adjacent literature outside the 42-study set. A Digital-Operations-Sustainability (DOS) framework is proposed as a conceptual model whose five propositions are hypotheses for future testing, not validated relationships. Priorities for future work include dual-reviewer, prospectively registered evidence synthesis; standardized sustainability indicators; integration of AI with life cycle assessment; longitudinal validation; and evidence from small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and developing economies.
